utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the Registrar to call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14AR 108 bis, Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. My name is Louise Arbour, I am the Prosecutor and appearing with me is Mr. Mark Harmon. May I just please inform the court that Mr. James Crawford, who is assisting the Prosecution, could not be in attendance but would be available tomorrow morning if he could be of assistance to the court at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: I am Ambassador Simonovic and I will be representing the Croatian government and delivering a statement on behalf of government. Our legal counselors are David Rivkin and Mr. Lee Casey, and the gentleman on my right is Dr Ivo Josipovic, who is a legal expert in the field of international criminal and procedural law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. My name is Russell Hayman and I appear with my colleague, Anto Nobile, on behalf of the accused General Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me first of all ask Mr. Blaskic if he can hear me. May I ask you to repeat? I understand I should repeat what I asked. I was asking whether he could hear me in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I hear you fine and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me start by pointing out that as you may remember, in our decision of 12th August 1997, we invited the applicant and the Prosecution to make submissions on both the admissibility and the merits of the application for appellate review by the Republic of Croatia, dated 25th July 1997, so therefore I would like first of all to turn to the Prosecution and ask whether the Prosecutor has any issues relating to admissibility to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: We do not, your Honour. Thank you very much. We have no submissions on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can therefore proceed as follows. May I suggest to you the following procedure: I would like, on behalf of my colleagues of the Appeal Chamber, to first of all ask the Republic of Croatia to briefly sum up their main points, say 25 minutes, a maximum of 20 minutes, and I say so because actually the briefs have been thorough and detailed so all the major issues have been thrashed out, both in your briefs and the briefs or the reply of the Prosecutor, so therefore I would urge you to simply, as I say, sum up your main points. After that, I think the Judges will ask a few questions and then we will move on to the Prosecution; again we would like to ask the Prosecution to briefly sum up their main points in 20 minutes and then we will ask questions. Then we will ask the Defence counsel whether they have any statements or points to make, and, of course, there will be questions also of Defence counsel if they decide to make any points. After that, we will have a second round and we will start again with Croatia and we will ask the Republic of Croatia to briefly make a sort of closing statement, followed by the Prosecution, and then by Defence counsel. Is this procedure acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We shall invest our efforts to be short as you have scheduled. We might slightly exceed, but we will do our best not to exaggerate, with your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on behalf of the government of the Republic of Croatia, I would like to express my gratitude to you for hearing this appeal. The question that is before you is of paramount importance for my country, but it also has far reaching consequences for the future development of international criminal law and international relations. The holding of this hearing and inviting submissions of amici curiae once again shows that the court is aware of the importance and sensitivity of its task. Your Honours, the Republic of Croatia as a victim of aggression played an important role in the founding of the Tribunal. We welcome the efforts of the Tribunal and its officers and we hope that the work of the Tribunal shall eventually reflect the true nature of the conflict. The government of Croatia regards co-operation with the Tribunal as its legal, political and moral obligation. Croatia's resistance to the use of subpoena in respect of a State and its high officials when acting in their official capacity is not resistance to co-operation; rather it arises out of a legitimate claim that such co-operation be conducted within the scope of jurisdiction of the Tribunal and with due respect to the sovereignty of the States involved. Your Honours, after these brief opening remarks, let me come to the point. Croatia regards issuing subpoenas to States and state officials, when they are acting in their official capacity, to be legally unfounded, logically inconsistent and politically unacceptable. Subpoenas are legally unfounded because neither the Statute of the Tribunal, relevant resolutions of the Security Council, nor international law provide the Tribunal with the power to issue a subpoena against the State. If the Security Council wished to create such a new and, let me say, revolutionary practice, it would have done it explicitly. Invoking alleged inherent powers of the Tribunal in this regard represents disrespect towards international law and towards the exclusive prerogatives of the Security Council. Subpoenas are logically inconsistent because the only possible outcome of a State's failure to co-operate, no matter whether it relates to an action designated as request for co-operation, order or even a subpoena, is reporting of the matter to the Security Council. Two points arise from this. Firstly, there is no sanction available at the level of the Tribunal since reporting of the matter to the Security Council cannot be regarded as such. Any consideration in respect of a possible sanction is reserved for the deliberations of the Security Council. Secondly, the available response to non-compliance at the level of the Tribunal is the same, irrespective of whether it relates to an action designated as request for co-operation, order or subpoena. There are no differentiating characteristics which would justify the use of the term "subpoena". Therefore the practice of calling a particular request for co-operation or an order a subpoena is clearly arbitrary and without any legal or logical justification. Finally, subpoenas are politically unacceptable to the Republic of Croatia, as they would be to most other States, as they challenge its sovereignty and equal treatment. There is not a single case of a subpoena ever having been issued to a sovereign state in this context. There is no support for the creation of such a precedent, either in the Statute of the Tribunal or under international law and practice. Croatia will not accept being treated contrary to the principle of the sovereign equality of States. Croatia rejects the discriminatory line of reasoning that while subpoenas are generally inapplicable to States, they can be applied to Croatia, particularly since the Security Council has not given such authority to the Tribunal. Your Honours, after demonstrating inapplicability of subpoena against States, let me now address the issue of subpoena against individual governmental officials. High government officials, when acting in their capacity, official capacity, cannot be distinguished from the State; therefore, a subpoena is equally inapplicable. Purporting to sanction high government officials acting in their official capacity is simply an attempt to circumvent Tribunal's inability to sanction the State. This notion that the Tribunal can issue a subpoena upon a State's high official to obtain state documents, including documents of sensitive national security character, is equally unfounded in the Tribunal's Statute and international law as is a subpoena to a State. Furthermore, insisting that the Tribunal is entitled, when seeking documents, to avoid designated state authority by directly addressing an official of its own choice is more than just disrespect of internal organisation within a State. It is a rejection of a state's sovereignty in regard to its right to decide about the competence of its individual organs. Just as it is the international obligation of a State to co-operate with the Tribunal, so it is the sovereign right of the State to establish the channel of communication. It is upon the State to designate a specialised body to accord co-operation with the Tribunal or to waive its right to do so. Whatever choice the State makes, it has to be respected by the Tribunal. Your Honours, when creating this Tribunal, the Security Council was very concerned to make clear the scope of Tribunal's jurisdiction. When adopting its Statute, representatives of the Security Council made it very clear that the Tribunal is not entitled to create new law and practice, but rather that it should rely upon its Statute and established international law. This Tribunal has been created to strengthen the rule of law, certainly not to violate it. I firmly believe that you should have this in mind when deciding in this very sensitive matter. Your Honours, Croatia is fully aware that the Tribunal has to be efficient. Croatia fully supports the efficiency of the Tribunal, but not efficiency which disregards the most fundamental principles of international law, the principle of the state sovereignty and sovereign equality among States. The key of the Tribunal's efficiency lies with the effective co-operation with the States and increased pressure of Security Council, if they do not co-operate. This was the intent of the Security Council. It is what the Statute spells out, and it is in carrying out these duties that the Tribunal will continue to enjoy the full support of the Republic of Croatia. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: May it please the court, good morning, my name is Lee Casey, and I am appearing on behalf of the Republic of Croatia and I would like to address some of the legal issues involved on this appeal. The subpoena duces tecum issued by Trial Chamber II to the Republic of Croatia and its Defence Minister was in clear violation of the accepted rules of international law and practice, and exceeded the lawful authority conferred on the International Tribunal by its founding Statute. As the Appeals Chamber found in its decision on jurisdiction in the Tadic case, the International Tribunal was established by the Security Council as "a judicial organ", a court of law. One of the characteristics of a judicial organ is both the source and limit of its legitimate lawful authority. The possession of jurisdiction over the individual or entity to be affected, and the subject matter to be decided, is essential to the legitimate exercise of judicial power. By issuing a compulsory order to the Republic of Croatia, and to its Defence Minister, Trial Chamber II exceeded the International Tribunal's lawful legitimate authority. As it has itself acknowledged, the International Tribunal does not have jurisdiction over States. In this regard, the Tribunal's 1995 Yearbook explains that: "The Tribunal’s Statute, which was approved by the Security Council in Resolution 827 (1993) 'is the source of the Tribunal's jurisdiction,' and 'the Statute does not, however, give the Tribunal personal jurisdiction over entities, such as States, organisations and associations.'" At no point does the ICTY Statute, either expressly or by implication, grant the International Tribunal jurisdiction over States. Ancillary or incidental jurisdiction cannot serve as a substitute for a primary jurisdiction or grant, as incorrectly suggested by both the Prosecution and Trial Chamber II. A court's ancillary jurisdiction can be used only in aid of its primary jurisdiction, and only with respect to individuals or entities that are otherwise subject to its legal authority. Indeed, if courts could issue subpoenas (or other orders) to individuals or entities beyond their jurisdiction based upon the pretext of exercising some ancillary jurisdiction, then any court, domestic or international, would be entitled to issue binding process to any individual entity or government anywhere in the world. This simply is not the law. The entire system of international co-operation using "requests for assistance" and "letters rogatory" has developed for the very reason that both domestic courts and international tribunals are limited by their subject-matter and personal jurisdiction, and cannot issue legally binding orders to individuals or entities, including States, otherwise beyond their jurisdiction. Consequently, however broadly the ICTY Statute is interpreted, it cannot support the issuance of a compulsory order by the International Tribunal to a State, an entity entirely beyond its legal authority. Both Trial Chamber II and the Prosecution have asserted that the power to issue compulsory orders for the production of documents, whether or not called a subpoena, is found in most legal systems, and that the International Tribunal therefore "has the inherent power to compel the production of documents necessary for a proper execution of its judicial function". Although most courts may have the authority to issue orders for the production of evidence -- although not the very unique type of subpoena duces tecum issued by Trial Chamber II to Croatia -- no court may issue such an order on a compulsory basis to an individual or entity not subject to its lawful jurisdiction. Moreover, the International Tribunal is an international court. There is no precedent for an International Tribunal issuing compulsory orders under threat of sanction to a State. In fact, the ability of international tribunals to obtain documentary evidence from States is highly limited. The leading international case authority in this area is the International Court of Justice's ruling in the Corfu Channel case, a case where the court requested from Great Britain certain documents that it thought would be useful to resolution of the matter. The United Kingdom refused to deliver those documents and indeed instructed its witnesses to refuse to answer questions regarding them. The court properly respected this refusal, and declined to draw any conclusions against Britain based on the fact that the documents were not produced. There is no warrant in either law or reason for the application of a different rule to Croatia. Both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution have sought to avoid these settled rules of law by suggesting that the International Tribunal is not subject to the accepted rules of domestic or international law because it was established as an enforcement measure pursuant to Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter. This extraordinary claim is manifestly incorrect. The authority to formulate and adopt Chapter VII enforcement measures against a State represents the very highest of the Security Council's power. Its use involves fundamentally political decisions that are themselves antithetical to the International Tribunal's judicial character. At no point did the Security Council even purport to vest the International Tribunal with such vast power. Indeed, it is very doubtful whether the Security Council could have delegated the authority to formulate and adopt Chapter VII enforcement measures to any other body, since such a delegation would deprive the five permanent members of the Security Council of their right to exercise a veto with respect to any particular measure. Consequently, the Tribunal does not have, and cannot exercise, the lawful authority to formulate and implement compulsory, coercive measures vis-a-vis States, whether in the form of orders or otherwise. The relationship of States to the International Tribunal is, in fact, governed by ICTY Statute Article 29, which requires States to co-operate with the International Tribunal and to comply with certain requests for assistance and orders issued by a Trial Chamber. Significantly, Article 29 does not purport to bring States within the Tribunal's jurisdiction or competence, nor does it constitute a grant of authority to the International Tribunal with respect to States. Rather, it is addressed directly to States (and not to the Tribunal), requiring them to co-operate with the Tribunal and to assist it in the implementation of its orders. Without Article 29, States would have had no such obligation. Significantly, Article 29 does not provide any authority for the International Tribunal to sanction a State that fails to carry out its obligations, and no such authority can be found in any other provision of the ICTY Statute. This is hardly surprising, since the ICTY was not vested with either personal jurisdiction over a State, or with the subject-matter jurisdiction or competence necessary for it to determine whether any particular State has, or has not, complied with its international law obligations. This authority would, however, be essential to any determination by the Tribunal that a State has not carried out its responsibilities vis-a-vis the International Tribunal, and to the imposition of any sanction upon a State or its officials. Trial Chamber II also has erred in ruling that a subpoena duces tecum could be issued to an individual state official, requiring the official to take actions within his official capacity, and that such an official could be required to appear before the Trial Chamber to explain any non-compliance. States, and not individuals, are the subjects of international law. To the extent that States (including Croatia) have international law obligations, those obligations are a charge upon the State, not upon individual state officers. Consequently, the International Tribunal can address itself (that is can issue a order or make a request that might trigger a State's obligations under Article 29), only to a State. It cannot issue directives to the state's officials requiring them personally to take some official action on behalf of their State, and calling them to account if their State fails to do as it is told. Not surprisingly, there is no international law precedent for holding the individual officials of a State accountable either for the execution of a state's international law obligations, or for their violation. And, in this respect, Trial Chamber II correctly held that individual state officers could not personally be sanctioned for the failure of their State to comply with the Tribunal's orders. The same legal and practical considerations that led the Trial Chamber to hold that individual officers cannot be sanctioned for failing to comply with an order apply equally to summoning them to appear before the Tribunal. Finally, the Appeals Chamber should consider the astonishing implications of the Prosecution's assertions that the International Tribunal may issue orders to individual state officials requiring them to exercise their government offices in a particular manner. Under the Prosecution's theory, these orders could require any action that the Tribunal might deem necessary to achieve its mission, up to and including any level of force the Tribunal may consider to be appropriate. Mere considerations of domestic law, foreign policy and national security would be entirely irrelevant. The officials of any State that failed to obey would be subject to whatever sanction the court might see fit to impose, whether it be a fine, imprisonment or removal from office. Again, the constitutional, legal or political arrangements of the State in question would be of no consequence. It is inherently incredible to suggest that the Security Council either vested or intended to vest the International Tribunal with such unlimited and unprecedented power. Significantly, the Prosecution has not denied either the nature or the extent of the power it claims for the International Tribunal. Indeed, the Prosecution itself has been unable to identify any legal limits on the power it claims. It has, of course, suggested that the "mandatory compliance power expressly conferred by Article 29(2) of the Statute will rarely, if ever, need to be invoked with respect to" States beyond the territory limits of the former Yugoslavia. The Prosecution states, "these compliance powers should be used against States when this is really necessary". Those nations not today in the Prosecution's sights should take cold comfort from these assurances. They may well wish to reflect that "necessity" is a justification that is inherently incapable of limitation; it cannot be quarantined. The Appeals Chamber should definitively reject the Prosecution's assertions that the International Tribunal may issue orders to individual state officials requiring them to exercise their government offices in a particular manner, or face sanction if they refuse to comply. The Trial Chamber also has incorrectly concluded that the issuance of what is, in fact, an United States-style third party "discovery" device, known as a "subpoena duces tecum", is a valid exercise of its authority to issue orders. Although the Prosecution has urged the Appeals Chamber not to examine the substance or terms of the subpoena duces tecum at issue here, the nature and form of Trial Chamber II's subpoena are very much in issue. From the very beginning of this process, Croatia has strongly objected to both the suggestion that the Trial Chamber could issue a compulsory order to a State, and to a particular form of order sought by the Prosecution in this case. Moreover, a detailed examination of the substance of the subpoena is necessary to the disposition of two arguments raised by the Prosecution, that the authority to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a State is inherent in the authority of all courts, and hence may be implied by the International Tribunal, and that the Tribunal has the "express" power to issue subpoenas and orders, and so also must be authorised to issue a subpoena duces tecum like that issued by Trial Chamber II. Whatever the Tribunal's authority to issue compulsory orders may be, it cannot be assumed that it is authorised to issue the type of subpoena duces tecum at issue here. The subpoena duces tecum sought by the Prosecutor, and issued by the Trial Chamber here, is in form and substance fundamentally different from the orders most national courts may issue requiring production of evidence for trial. It has not, as the Prosecution suggests, existed since Late Antiquity. Rather, the subpoena duces tecum issued to Croatia is in form and substance an American-style civil discovery request, a coercive order issued to a non-party and requiring the production of documents that may or may not exist, and that may or may not be relevant to the issues before the court. It is a classic fishing expedition. Indeed, the fishing expedition nature of the Prosecution's requests in this case are revealed by its own admissions that it has requested these records merely because they are the sorts of documents that States normally maintain, not because they are documents known to exist, to be relevant to the Blaskic Prosecution, and unavailable from any other source. Far from representing the normal, "inherent" or accepted authority of all courts, the American rules have not been widely copied outside the United States. Their application beyond the United States (particularly in the form of a subpoena duces tecum) has been highly controversial. By the same token, the reference to Article 29(2) to "orders for the production of evidence" cannot be assumed to mean the issuance of a US-style subpoena duces tecum. Its most probable meaning, in accordance with general practice beyond the United States, is that the Tribunal may issue orders to the parties before it requiring them to produce evidence known to exist and that is necessary for trial but not otherwise available to the requesting party. In reaching its decision, the Trial Chamber accepted the Prosecutor's arguments of necessity, and asserted that "the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal dictates that the evidence which it requires will often be in the form of government documents". This is by no means manifest. Most of the world's courts function effectively and fairly without the ability to compel States, or even individuals, "to submit whatever material is necessary to evaluate" the case before them. Croatia has declined to provide the documents demanded by the Prosecutor in part because they may obtain information of national security concern. Both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor have suggested that any such concerns must be subject to review and resolution by the Trial Chamber, much as claims of a national security "privilege" are resolved in national courts. However, the right of certain national courts to review and determine the "executive privilege" or "national security" claims of their own governments has no analogue or application in international law. The determination of the national security needs of each State is a fundamental attribute of its sovereignty. An international tribunal cannot judge and determine such claims like a domestic court determining claims of "privilege". In international fora like the ICJ, for example, a State's assertion of national security interests is universally respected, even where the State is within the competence of the court; again, the Corfu Channel case is the leading example in this area. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber's opinion in this regard begins from the mistaken premise that an International Tribunal may act as do some national courts, determining whether confidential government documents may be used in litigation or revealed to the public. The authority of national courts to judge national security claims by their own States, however, cannot serve as a basis for the exercise of this power by the International Tribunal. Although domestic courts may be entitled to weigh the national security claims made by their own governments, this is a matter entirely dependent upon the constituted form of government involved. In all such circumstances, the Judges who assess national security claims are a part of the legitimately constituted government of such States, and are accountable as such. The Tribunal should accept and follow the well settled international practice, as found in the Corfu Channel case, to respect the national security claims of States, for there is not authority in law or reason that would support a different rule for Croatia. In conclusion, the International Tribunal does not have the power to issue a subpoena duces tecum, or any other compulsory order under threat of sanction, to a State. This is the conclusion required by the accepted norms of public international law and by the International Tribunal's Statute. Moreover, the International Tribunal cannot infer this power. The subpoena duces tecum is not a process inherent in all legal systems. In addition, the International Tribunal can neither issue a subpoena duces tecum to the officials of a State, sanction those officials if they fail to comply with such an order, or summon them to explain their State's failure to comply. Under the established rules of international law, States alone are responsible for complying with their international obligations, and individual officials cannot be held hostage for their State's good behaviour. For all of the reasons stated above, the Republic of Croatia asks the Appeal Chamber to reverse Trial Chamber II's decision on the objection of the Republic of Croatia to the issuance of a subpoena duces tecum 18 July 1997, and to instruct the Trial Chambers and the Prosecutor that no further compulsory orders under threat of sanction may be issued to States or their officials, and to quash the subpoena duces tecum issued by Trial Chamber II to the Republic of Croatia and its and its Defence Minister. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will ask a few questions. My colleagues were so kind as to suggest that I should start by putting questions and I countersuggested that for the proper discussion of the various issues we should probably divide up the whole cluster of problems into five categories. I suggest the following categories: (1) preliminary questions; (2) orders, binding orders to States; (3) binding orders to state officials; (4) binding orders to individuals; and (5), the question of national security concerns. Therefore I propose that I will start by asking questions relating to the first issue, preliminary issues, and then turn to my colleagues to see whether they have questions on the same issue and after that, we move on to the second class of problems, so as to have a well-organised and orderly discussion. Let me start with what I call preliminary questions. I have one question which to my mind is preliminary to the other questions which we will discuss, namely the question of whether or not the Appeals Chamber should enter into and discuss the matter of legal remedies or sanctions in case of non-compliance with binding orders of the Tribunal. You may have noticed that I on purpose used the neutral word "binding orders" and I on purpose avoid the word "subpoena". Of course, in your brief and the reply, the Republic of Croatia stresses time and again that the question of the power of our Tribunal to issue binding orders is closely intertwined with the issue of what sanctions or remedies should be provided for in any case of non-compliance. You may have noticed that the Trial Chamber, however, decided in its decision that this issue is not ripe for consideration, and the Prosecutor, in response to the brief of the Republic of Croatia, in paragraphs 23 and 24, pointed out that in her view, these review proceedings -- an issue that does not arise in these review proceedings is the question of potential penalties or remedies for non-compliance with a subpoena. According to the Prosecution, therefore, it is not for the Appeals Chamber to enter into or discuss this matter. I wonder whether you could comment on the importance of the issue of penalties or remedies. I see two sides to this problem. I would say one side relates to the doctrine of ripeness, which has been taken up by the Trial Chamber, the doctrine, as we all know, is an American doctrine and whether or not this doctrine can apply to our case and then more generally, and then I would like to draw upon the competence of Ambassador Simonovic, who before being Ambassador was a distinguished Professor of jurisprudence, and to go also into this matter, whether or not we accept the American doctrine of ripeness, whether or not it is possible to try to identify a substantive rule without going into the question of what legal remedy may or may not accompany that rule and be applicable in case of non-compliance with the substantive rule. Shall we first of all address the issue of ripeness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour. I think your Honour is absolutely correct that the question of ripeness is a doctrine that arises, indeed it arises out of the United States' constitution's requirement that no federal court may issue a decision where there is not an actual controversy, a case or controversy that is amenable to the court's decision. As a result, American courts have developed the doctrine of ripeness in their attempts to determine whether or not there is an actual controversy currently to be decided. If they discover that there is not, then the constitution prohibits them from actually making a decision. It is very questionable, indeed I think it is probably not the case, that this doctrine has any application in international law which, of course, is not, although both the American constitution and international law have their perhaps roots arguably in 18th century ideas of natural law, this particular, very particular doctrine does not apply to the current state of international law very well, and so I think the court would be well advised to determine that it simply does not apply here. If your Honour would like, I will also address the actual application in this case. Trial Chamber II did indeed in its opinion suggest that the question of penalties was not ripe for determination. It did, however, indicate very specifically that penalties could and would be assessed if there was a refusal to comply. Even in the United States, where the doctrine of ripeness applies, in that sort of situation one would at least be able to get a declaratory judgment from a court. Where one is in fact actually subject to a real threat of such a sanction one is not required to go ahead and disobey the order to determine whether an actual sanction will be imposed. But one may go into court and ask the court for a declaratory judgment, so you are not put in that difficult position, and the court will issue the judgment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to go on the same issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may, on the same issue, your Honour. The point that I would like to make, and I believe we made it in our written submissions, is that there is a very logical nexus between the inability of a Tribunal to prescribe appropriate sanctions against States, and our argument that holding the State subject to a jurisdiction is not a proper exercise of judicial power. I can elaborate if you want, but in essence, that point is very helpful to the central argument we are making relevant to the lack of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. When I was referring to the more general theoretical issue, and I mentioned Ambassador Simonovic, I was thinking of some legal theories which have been propounded in this century by the two probably most distinguished professors or scholars specialising in jurisprudence, Hans Kelsen and Hart, the English Hart. We all know that both of them insisted that you cannot identify a substantive rule without also focusing on the proper remedy. You remember in Hart you have the distinction between primary and secondary rules and this distinction is also relevant to us in international law, because to some extent it was taken up by the International Law Commission in the report by Ago on State responsibility, so I wonder there whether, leaving aside the American doctrine of ripeness, it is possible, not only from a theoretical viewpoint but also from the inherent concept of law, to again distinguish the two issues, whether or not there is a substantive rule providing for a power of our Tribunal, say, to impose sanctions on the one side or to impose upon a country, a State, a certain behaviour. And then the different question of what happens if that particular country or State does not comply with the substantive rule imposing a legal obligation. Can we distinguish -- in your opinion, could such a distinction be acceptable, even from this different viewpoint, which is a rather different viewpoint, as I say, a theoretical view point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I think not, your Honour. It is true that both in American law and indeed in common law there are concepts of damage without legal injury or a legal cause, potentially without a remedy, but I do not think that those doctrines would apply in international law. It really is quite impossible to make a distinction, particularly when you are talking about a compulsory order of any sort, between the power to issue the order and the remedy. There must be some remedy. The remedy may well be not imprisonment, it may not be a fine, but there must indeed be some sanction. Indeed, the Trial Chamber itself stated that, that there would be a sanction. If it were merely in the Trial Chamber's view to report the matter to the Security Council, that, of course, would be a very grave sanction, because, at least in the Trial Chamber's view,, it would also have involved a judicial determination that Croatia had indeed violated its international obligations, and that is indeed a very severe, serious matter. So that, in fact, it seems really not to be possible to make this clean distinction which often one indeed does see in American cases; one will even try liability and damages separately. It is very common to try separately those two. I do not think that has application in international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are dealing with such a complex issue that probably a number of books will be written on this very subject matter, and I hope one of them will be yours. Concerning the issue of sanction, it is an old theoretical problem; is there any rule without a sanction? The best answer I could find in legal theory is that there is a legal rule if there is established an organ who can then be in charge to issue a sanction, which does not mean that it is a sanction but there is an organ which can then impose a sanction. I think that this is clearly the case, so you have the Rules of the Tribunal, you have Statute of the Tribunal and Rules of Procedure, and when there is no sanction, the theoretical answer would be "those are legal rules, they are binding because there is an organ which is entitled to impose a sanction". That would be, I think, the theoretical answer derived from legal theory and especially Kelsen and Hart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. I would like to ask my colleagues whether they have any questions on this first of our problems, namely preliminary questions. Of course, I also suggest that the very notion of subpoena may be discussed at this stage, whether or not we should go on using the word "subpoena" or, as the Trial Chamber itself suggested, we could use the word subpoena but with a neutral meaning, namely legally binding orders by the Tribunal. I wonder whether there are any questions? Judge Li?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to ask a question. The question is this: I would like to know why the OTP choose to apply for a subpoena duces tecum instead of for an order directing Croatia to produce the documents, because Article 29(2) of our Statute provides that this Tribunal can only request or order a State to produce documents. It does not expressly State that a subpoena can be issued to a sovereign State, so I think it is necessary for the OTP to explain the reason why the OTP chose to apply for a subpoena instead of applying for an order. This is my first question. Then the second, I would like to know whether the term "subpoena" can be understood to mean a binding order, instead of its original meaning of "under penalty in case of non-compliance", as used in the common law systems. If it can be understood, that is if "subpoena" can be understood as a "binding order", please give the reasons why it can be understood so, why it can be so understood. Thank you. The OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Judge Li, may I ask you, with all due respect, whether we could ask later on this question to the Prosecution, when we move on to the Prosecution? We try now to concentrate on questions to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: I understand. This question is to be asked later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to address the second part of the Judge's question. Obviously the first part is for the Prosecution. I think in fact that whatever we call the process, the order that has been issued, it is nevertheless a compulsory order which carries with it the threat, indeed the promise, of sanction for its denial; whether you call that a subpoena or whether you call it a compulsory order, at least as it has been issued here, it is an order under threat of sanction, and consequently, at least with respect to the subpoena, the order that is currently before the court, it is clearly an order under threat of sanction regardless what we may choose to call it. Obviously, in the court's determination of what power it may have to issue orders, it may well find that it has the authority to issue orders but that such orders may not be compulsory. One obviously must get in then to the whole question of whether, as your Honour was raising, there can be an order that does not carry with it some threat of sanction, since to be an order of itself it must be somehow enforceable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. With your agreement, I would like now to suggest that we move on to the second of the issues which I proposed before, namely the question of whether or not our Tribunal has the authority to address binding orders. On this score I have three questions to ask you. First of all, I am not clear about how you actually interpret Article 29 of our Statute, which seems, on its face, to be crystal clear in providing for the authority of our Tribunal to issue binding orders which must be complied with by States, by any State. You do not even find there a qualification, "Member States of the UN", any State member of the international community ia addressed, so your interpretation on Article 29 and how do you reconcile this interpretation with the opposition? My second question relates to what you have pointed out on page 40 and 41 of your brief, your brief of 18th August. May I read out just one passage which was a bit puzzling to me. You say, and I quote: "Our interpretation fully comports with the language and purpose of Article 29. The types of requests for assistance and orders listed in Article 29 all involve orders to act upon individuals within the Tribunal’s competence, not States. As noted above, Article 29 requires States to comply with requests for assistance or orders issued by the Trial Chamber “including, but not limited to”, the identification, location, arrest, detention or surrender of individuals who are themselves within the Tribunal's competence." If I understand you correctly, you mean to say that Croatia is duty bound to comply with an order which relates to the behaviour of Croatia vis-a-vis an individual, say a witness or an indictee. Therefore if our Tribunal orders Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, to arrest an indictee or to compel a witness to come forward, then you are covered by this obligation; whereas this obligation does not concern your behaviour as a State with regard to the production by Croatia itself of documents which are needed for our trial. But I feel that this distinction is really artificial, because in any case -- I would like you to comment on that -- you have an obligation relating to the behaviour of Croatian state organs. In one case, say, Croatian state organs have to arrest somebody or to compel somebody to come forward and testify before our Tribunal, or you are requested to search, say, the premises of one of our suspects or indictees, so this is behaviour by state organs. I do not see why then you make a distinction between the behaviour of state organs relating to their own documents, because, in any case, those documents may be needed, documents which are in the hands of Croatian state organs, may be needed for the purpose of our trials, because they may be evidence or they are crucial evidence. So how do you make this distinction, on what is it based since, as I say, with all due respect, to me it seems an extremely artificial distinction which you do not find in Article 29. Article 29 gives a blanket obligation upon all States of the international community to comply without undue delay with any order or request of the Tribunal. You do not find that distinction there which you try to set out in your brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that first and foremost Article 29 has to be interpreted within the court's jurisdiction. It does not give the court jurisdiction over States; again, as I mentioned earlier, it is addressed to States from the Security Council, not to the Tribunal. Therefore when you come about interpreting what Article 29 says and means, you have to start out from the proposition that States are not subject to the court's authority, so that a binding order would not be -- the court could not issue a binding order to the States, just as it could not issue a binding order to some individual who was not, for whatever reason, within its personal jurisdiction, someone living in another continent who never had anything to do with the former Yugoslavia. In terms of the actual distinction under (2), when you come at it from that basis, I think there is a very significant distinction. What (2) does is it acts as, very commonly, treaties will set out. It creates an obligation of a State to assist what is in effect a foreign tribunal in carrying out its orders, request for assistance and orders, and it is very common. The court of one State may need evidence from an individual living in another State who is otherwise beyond its jurisdiction. It cannot simply issue a binding order ordering a citizen of Brazil to come to France to give testimony, it has to approach the courts or government, depending on how it is set up, and ask their assistance in essentially ordering this individual to come. The court in Brazil may well do that or it may refuse to do that. If it refuses to do that, it is not subject to sanction by the French court asking; it may well, however, depending on whether there is a treaty between France and Brazil, be in violation of its international obligation, that is quite possible, but the French court obviously could not make a determination as to that and we would submit that neither could the International Tribunal, since the question of whether a State is or is not in violation of international law also is not within its stated competence. Further, as to the actual distinction between an order that is issued to a State, of which it is itself the object, and the other kinds of orders that Article 29(2) actually address, again if the court will note, all of these types of orders do act upon individuals, they do not act upon States. States clearly have an international law obligation to help you execute those orders, but there is, we would submit, a very significant difference between an order to an individual within your competence, the State must help you execute, and an order to the State itself requiring it to do something for which there is no precedent in international law, and that is of itself not like the things that are stated in Article 29. So that that is really the distinction, the significant distinction. Ambassador, did you have something you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one clarification. This difference we heard about concerned a situation where a request, probable request, has no connection with trials here in the court, because we found some of the requests, some of the wishes from the Prosecutor out of the Judges' scope. What we think about this is that the Republic of Croatia completely accepts all orders and we feel obliged by your orders, but what the Republic of Croatia does not accept is the form of subpoena, because it is contrary to international law, including your Statute. Secondly, this theory about "subpoena" without "poena" is in our opinion the same thing as apple pie without apple. That is the reason why we would like to stress and ask you to put down very clearly that this court has power to issue binding orders. The Republic of Croatia accepts that, but not the form of subpoena. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask a question from the last speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Does that mean, your statement, that an order to a State to produce specific documents, narrowly defined, with the only result of non-compliance being, conceivably, a report of that non-compliance to the Security Council --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: -- would be a situation that you would regard as entirely appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that in accordance with the Statute and accepted rules of international law, that is the only remedy. It is a very severe remedy and Croatia is very aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is still related to Article 29(2). I wonder whether you can give any assistance to the expression at (2), "with any request for assistance or an order issued by a Trial Chamber", that phrase. What is your own interpretation of that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, as it is written, it requires States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance, we all know what request for assistance means, or an order issued by the Trial Chamber. I would submit that request for assistance is the normal request by a government or an international organisation to another government, asking for its assistance in executing orders or in other ways; and in addition, this does impose a binding obligation on States to execute other orders issued by the Trial Chamber, the type of which are listed. Again, all the orders listed are addressed to, or deal with, individuals who are otherwise within the Trial Chamber's competence, so that essentially, in many ways, Article 29 merely serves the purpose of what some multilateral and many bilateral treaties serve and that is to create an international obligation. They require States to receive requests for assistance, to consider them and to act upon them and to execute these orders. It does not, however, impose an obligation on States that can be the subject of sanction; indeed, even if a State refuses to comply with an order that is within the accepted framework of (2), there would be no sanction provided, none is provided in Article 29. Again, the State may well be in violation of its international obligations, but as in so many cases, there is no sanction provided for that, at least -- I should say no judicial sanction. There may well be consequences to be paid on the political, the relations between States or between that State and the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I asked this question because if you observe the word "or", there is a disjunctive and then it continues by "including but not limited to", which expands the category of things which could be done under (2).

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: That is very true, but what you have here is a list of the types of orders they had in mind. It is not an exhaustive list, but if you are going to add to the list, you are going to have to add orders like the ones that are listed, which again -- orders for the arrest of someone, orders for the taking of testimony or the production of evidence -- again, that is somewhat ambiguous, but in terms of the taking of testimony it is clearly from individuals who are otherwise within the Trial Chamber's competence. The production of evidence I think would have to be interpreted in the same way, again within the context where it is found. One might also point out, of course, that the production of evidence does not say the production of documents, the production of state documents. The court may interpret evidence broadly, but evidence does not necessarily incorporate those very specific kinds of materials. You may well be talking about an order asking a State to assist in the gathering of material evidence, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The way you interpret it is seeing if (a) to (e) constitutes a generis. There is no generis in these, because they are all quite separate items. You cannot use the ejusdum generis rule to say that. It has to fall within this category of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I guess, your Honour, I would submit that it does create a generis. All of the orders here are types of orders that get served on individuals, arrest warrants, you arrest an individual, you take an individual's testimony, you serve a document on an individual, you arrest or detain an individual, or States must surrender and transfer the accused. All of the types of orders are actually directed at the action of the order that takes place on an individual who is otherwise within the Tribunal's competence. I guess I would submit that it does create a generis here and the ejusdum generis rule is indeed applicable to interpreting this Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Just an additional remark. It is more of an academic discussion relating to Article 29. It does not change our general position, that the court is perfectly entitled to issue binding orders, including orders to bring documents to the court, so in a sense, we are not in principle objecting to our obligation to present documents, certainly within the scope of the established international law, certainly with certain limitations that are related to national security concerns of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Li?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question. Will you please explain the meaning of fishing expedition? Do all the documents required to be produced by Croatia belong to this category? If not all of these documents belong to this category, then what documents belong to this category and what documents do not belong to this category? I would like you to state clearly which of the documents required Croatia to produce belong to this category. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the meaning of the term -- the term "fishing expedition" is a colloquial expression that is very often applied to the kinds of subpoenas that are at issue here. It basically means that the Prosecution does not really know what documents it is asking for. It is asking for many very broad categories of documents. It does not actually know whether those categories even exist, let alone whether they may contain documents that are relevant to the trial of the defendant. In American law, it is very common for someone to file a law suit with very minimal evidence and then to use this type of discovery request in the hope that they may be able to support their case with evidence they find from the defendant or from another party, and the Rules of procedure allow them to do that. Again, that has no application in international law and has been rejected by most of the world's countries very dramatically and indeed a number of nations have actually enacted laws that forbid the application of that kind of process coming from the United States in their countries. We would submit that all of the documents that the Prosecution is seeking would fall into that category. The Prosecution does not really know what documents it is seeking. It has asked for these many categories of documents, some which may exist, some which may not, some documents that are relevant, some which are not, it simply does not know, and it is using this as an attempt to essentially investigate the case after the indictment has been brought down. That is basically what we mean by "fishing expedition".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it that, according to your view, all the documents required belong to this category; that is, all belong to this category of fishing expedition, and if this is your view, do you mean that every requirement of producing a document constitutes a fishing expedition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I just add a footnote to what Judge Li asked? I think for the proper conduct of our proceedings, we should not enter into the specifics of the request by the Prosecution, because this is not proper for us. The Appeals Chamber should only pass upon the general concept of "binding order" and should not deal with that particular -- this is a point made and I agree with the Prosecutor, in the Prosecution's brief. We should not enter into this specific subpoena issued by the Trial Chamber, the contents and the list of documents whether or not -- could you therefore respond to Judge Li in general terms, without any specific reference to that particular subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will attempt to do that. First I would like to respond to your statement. I think the court actually does have to look at the actual terms of this subpoena. The arguments here made to support the court's general authority, to issue subpoenas of this sort or of any sort, are that they are inherent in all courts and that you can imply -- you may find somewhere expressed in the Statute. In order to judge those arguments you are going to have to see what it is the Trial Chamber did, the actual order issued, because this is not an order like other orders, and so even if the court may find that the power to issue a subpoena or a binding order is inherent, it is not necessarily the case that this order is inherent, and that too is a general question. Obviously if the court were to decide that this kind of order in the form it is were appropriate, we would then indeed argue the details of the order based on this category and that category, and whether that is too broad, and, as for a protective order for those categories, is it too broad, but we are not at that level yet, and I think the Trial Chamber made a serious mistake when it attempted to paper over the actual type of order that was issued here and say, "You can just deal with that essentially in a discovery process below". The American rules of civil discovery do not apply here. Maybe you will decide that they ought to apply. I think you would make a very serious mistake based upon my experience with them, but you might decide that. In which case, then we would indeed go to those arguments. I do think you have to look at the details of the order here. In response to the Judge's question, there is indeed at least one category that we do not believe is part of a fishing expedition, but again, I will try not to get into the actual details of the order. It is the nature of the broadness of all the categories that is really the problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask another question? I would like to put another question to you. Can the reporting by this Tribunal to the Security Council of the non-compliance of a sovereign State with a subpoena be considered a sanction equivalent to the penalties threatened in a subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we think they may. Again, the sanctions for failing to comply with a subpoena may be -- certainly under domestic law they can be imprisonment, they can be a serious fine, but the decision by the court -- the court I should say is always free to approach the Security Council and say "this country or that country has not co-operated in the way that we think is appropriate and will you please take action". What the court cannot do is to make a judicial determination, a judicial finding that a particular country is in violation of its international obligations. That is simply not within its competence. It may well -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. This is actually a point I would like to raise. On pages 16 and 17 of your briefs you make this point, and I really do not understand why it is for the Security Council to determine, as you say, whether the State is in violation of its obligations and what action to take. I do not see why the Tribunal as a judicial institution should not be empowered to satisfy itself that a State is not in compliance with an international legal obligation. This is a typical judicial function. Why should we ask the Security Council, which is a political body, to make a judicial finding? I do understand that it is for the Security Council to take sanctions, if any, but I do not see why we should refrain from making any judicial determination. Could you explain your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Again, with respect, we believe that the court's jurisdiction does not cover judging whether States have or have not complied with their international obligations, either to the Tribunal or generally. It simply does not have the necessary jurisdictional grant in its Statute in order to make that kind of determination, to actually enter an adjudication saying "a State has violated" -- even though it is true, that is the kind of thing courts do, of course, it is a judicial type of determination, but the court has not been vested with the power in this case to make that kind of a judicial determination. That is why we say that it is ultimately for the Security Council to decide whether or not the State has violated its international obligations. You are, of course, perfectly free to go to the Security Council and say "we think they have indeed violated -- in our opinion they have violated international law", but what you cannot do is issue a judgment saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Actually then how would you explain the fact that on five different occasions, the President of this Tribunal, at the request of a Trial Chamber, did report to the Security Council that in the view of the Trial Chamber, a particular State had breached its international obligation by non-co-operation and there was no complaint or protest in the Security Council. Actually the Security Council took up the decision by a Trial Chamber and acted upon it by issuing what one could regard as a sanction, namely it deplored or even condemned on one or two occasions the attitude of that particular country. So therefore, in a way, if your theory was correct, one should speak here of a sort of acquiescence by the Security Council in a sort of misconduct by our Tribunal, a deviation from our judicial activity. I do not see how you could explain therefore the behaviour of the Security Council vis-a-vis our five reports -- I was simply sort of a messenger, I was simply reporting a judicial finding by a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ambassador Simonovic has a word. I would say it is very difficult to say why the Security Council may or may not have decided to do something. The doctrine of acquiescence is in itself a very slippery slope. You can never really tell why they did something like that. Again, the fact that it may well have happened in the past -- I am not sure we are imputing any improper action by the court, it is simply that this may not have come to the court's attention. The court may not have focused on the issue before. As far as I can tell, it has not been raised with a State as party to brief and argue the issue, so I think that would be -- the ambassador has something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: We do think that the court is in charge of finding whether there is compliance or that there is not compliance. It is certainly extremely embarrassing for a State that such a finding gets made, but from a procedural point of view, it is not a sanction. It is a procedural precondition for the other organ who is in charge then to establish whether it is a case where sanction could be used or not. It is also related to the theoretical problem we were discussing; are there any rules without sanctions? In general, no, but they are legal rules if there is an established and clearly indicated organ who is in charge of deciding about sanctions, so I would not consider the deliberation of a court to be a sanction itself. It is embarrassing by itself, but it is the procedural mean for forwarding the specific case to the Security Council who is in charge of deliberating on sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may just add one final point? Obviously, with respect to your example, in order for you to send something to the Security Council that is entirely consistent with your judicial dignity -- as Ambassador Simonovic pointed out, as a general process, for you to say, "Look, Security Council, we think this State or this entity have done something wrong, they have not complied", to say, "We do not think it constitutes a legally binding adjudication" is nothing more than to say that Security Council would be seized of all the issues de novo, and the Security Council is not and can never be an automatic rubber stamp, whose only function, without disturbing the results of your adjudication, is to sanction the State or not sanction the State. I would respectfully submit the Security Council is entirely free to look at all the facts and conclude that you are indeed wrong; that the particular action that you believe to be non-compliant is indeed compliant. Insofar as there are no limitations on the power of the Security Council to do anything, for you as the court to be in a situation where what you consider to be a binding adjudication to be overturned by the Security Council is, I would submit, in itself an indication that that was not a binding result. So it is not so much the forum in which you submit your report to the Security Council, it is rather what the Security Council is empowered to do at that time. Again, our view is anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it is very important to stress that if this court establishes the decision that any State does not co-operate well, that it is not likely that Security Council is going to decide differently. I hope they are going just to decide what kind of sanction is necessary or is any sanction necessary at all, but I think your decision will be proper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Before moving on, because I understand there are no other questions, to the third issue, binding orders to state officials, may I suggest that we break for coffee. I would like to adjourn, with the agreement of my colleagues, for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We now move on, I would like to just add, we move on to the third category, orders to state officials. There I have a few questions to ask you, hypothetical questions. Assuming the Tribunal cannot issue a binding order to a state official as such, acting in his official capacity, could the Tribunal however issue a binding order to a state official who, prior to becoming, say, a Minister of Defence or Minister of Foreign Affairs, happened to witness a crime or happened to be given an important document not in his official capacity, but only because he happened to be a friend of somebody who was in possession of this document? So this is the first case: could the Tribunal issue a binding order and summon this person who acted in this way? This is one instance. A second hypothetical situation is where a state official, in his official capacity, happens to witness, say, the transmission of an order which might amount to a crime, or order the commission of crimes, but he was, say, a Minister, but he was there present not in his official capacity and happened to see what happened, what occurred. Could one say that there he acted in his official capacity? If not, could he again be summoned to testify before the Tribunal? These are two questions, and I have a third question which -- maybe you could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I think clearly the court could issue a subpoena to an individual who witnessed an incident or saw documents before he was a state official, even though he may now be a state official. You would not be calling him in his official capacity, you would be calling him as an individual who would otherwise be subject to the court's jurisdiction, someone in the former Yugoslavia who had witnessed a crime in that territory, of course you could do that. In the second case, I think you would have to look at what the individual's official duties were, but very likely you could also issue a subpoena to him to come again and testify in his individual capacity as to what he saw. I think the only instance where there would be a question about whether you could do that would be, say, if it was the official job of the individual in question to monitor these official documents, and if it was somehow actually a core part of his function, then I think there would be a question whether you could call him, because it would be impossible -- you can always call him as an individual, but he could not talk without the permission of his State.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. My third hypothetical situation: a binding order is issued by the Tribunal to a State for the production of documents which are in the hands of a Minister, a state official exercising his official capacity. The State decides that that official should deliver those documents, send them to our Tribunal, but that state official refuses to comply with the instructions of his own government and the government is not in a position to compel him to comply with the instructions. Would you say that he is still acting in his official capacity as a state organ or might one think he is no longer state organ, he is refusing to exercise his official duties, because if he did exercise his official duties, he would comply with the request of his own government, and therefore in this particular situation, he may be the subject of a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I think in that situation first you would obviously have to look at whether the State was indeed -- ordinarily they make the decision, a Minister refuses, the Minister gets fired and a new Minister complies, it is fairly simple. In the situation you are positing where the State in question effectively, for whatever reason, does not have control over this individual and it would effectively come to the court in a plea for help and say "we cannot do anything about this, would you try to use your authority", perhaps in that case -- again, you would have to look at the actual facts and circumstances to determine things like is the individual -- one thing the State could indeed always do, indeed the simplest thing for them to do, is to say "okay, you will not do it, you are fired". He may still have the documents, they may not be able to make him produce the documents, the State may then come to you and say "he is all yours". Effectively, the State has rendered that person an individual who you can reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just one very short remark. What is considered as wrong in Trial Chamber II decision is that this requirement that high officials in every case comes to the court and describes what is going on in his country, so I think this is a proper procedure, when State is not able to ensure the compliance with your order then probably you can ask for this former official -- usually "former" because I cannot imagine the State having such official on his post. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there are any questions on this particular issue of state officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: State officials, yes. I would raise this question. If the government of a sovereign State forbids a high official of that State to comply with the binding order and that government does not offer any other means of assistance to this Tribunal, should not the responsibility of the resulting non-compliance with the binding order be borne by that State? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we think it should, with the exception of some very narrow circumstances. The international obligations of States are States -- the obligations of those States, not the individual obligations of their political leadership, and consequently, if a State is in violation of its international obligations, it is the State that must be looked to to either enforce against or again normally that may be anything from sanctions by the Security Council to a declaration of war by the offended State, but it is indeed the State's obligations and not the individual's. It is up to each State, obviously, to discipline their public officials and if someone takes action that puts their State in violation of its international obligations, again in most States that individual would at least be looking for new work and at worst might well suffer serious criminal penalties. But you are correct, it is indeed the State that one must look to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any questions? All right, so we can move on to the fourth class of questions, orders to individuals. There, if I may start, I would like to ask only one question: do you feel that the Tribunal has the power to issue binding orders to individuals, say, to summon them to come to The Hague and give testimony or to surrender to deliver documents? First question. And if they do not comply with such summons or order, may they be held in contempt of the Tribunal under the general principle of contempt of Tribunal, not in particular under Rule 77 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which has a very limited scope. Third question: if they may be held in contempt here at The Hague, do you think -- if they do not appear, of course, they do not come over here, do you think a trial in absentia may be held here to pass on their alleged contempt of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think as to the first question, with respect to individuals who are indeed otherwise within the tribunals, say not state officials at all, of course the Tribunal has jurisdiction over those individuals, can summon them, can issue subpoenas. Again, whether they could issue the kind of subpoena duces tecum issued here is another question. With respect to those persons, I do not see any reason why the court could not adopt those kind of rules. Again, I would advise strongly against it, but you could, and those individuals could then be compelled to either produce documents or come and testify. If they did not, your second question really goes to, does the court as a court have the inherent authority to issue what in common law jurisdiction would be called a civil contempt warrant, which would not be imposing "criminal penalties", but could nonetheless compel someone by even imprisonment until they decided to comply with the court's order. As to that question, domestic courts normally can do that. It varies by the system, of course, but -- let me speak to, at least in common law countries it is considered inherent for the court to be able to enforce that kind of order by civil contempt. Whether an international court could do that I think is perhaps a more difficult question, but it would -- I think a court would be within reason if it concluded that yes, as a court it does have that authority with respect to individuals who are otherwise within its competence. As to the third question, whether a trial in absentia could be held, that I think the court could clearly, after obviously -- it would comply with the requirement of due process, notification to the extent it was possible, perhaps by publication, that the individual was under an order to appear, I think it probably then could go ahead, at least with respect to that individual, and decide that he or she was in violation with the order and issue a civil contempt -- it would be a warrant in that case for their detention -- and what you would then do is send that warrant to the State that the individual happened to be in, asking that State to execute that order and to provide the individual here to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: May I just add a brief point, your Honour. Obviously this is not a particularly practical question as far as Croatia is concerned, because the facts are quite different, but since we are having a bit of an academic discussion, I would say it probably would be a good idea for a court to ascertain that the individual involved is alive and is in a position to comply with that order, because for example, if that individual -- let us say he is in prison, because for a country it would offend the fundamental norms of due process for that individual to suffer an additional penalty of civil contempt, so some factual investigation would be warranted but indeed, since we are talking about a civil process, a trial in absentia would not be fundamentally offensive, at least to an American style of due process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, but would you agree that in any case this would be a sort of fallback solution, because if an individual acting in his individual capacity is summoned to come here or to deliver documents he possesses and refuses to do so, the normal procedure would be for the Tribunal to request the relevant competent state authorities to try to enforce that particular order, and, as you know, most pieces of implementing legislation relating to our Tribunal provide for this right and power of state authorities to enforce orders at this level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not have any more questions. Any more questions on this point? Thank you. We now may move on to the fifth and final question which is rather important and tricky, national security concerns. There, if I may start, I would like to ask you to comment on one particular point. Both in your written submissions and today, you have insisted on the Corfu Channel case as an important precedent. However, you are aware that that decision was taken on the strength of Article 49 of the Statute of the ICJ, which simply States that the court may call upon a State to produce documents and it can take note of any refusal.
