So it is not termed in binding terms, so, therefore, I wonder to what extent this case or the Corfu Channel case might be mutatis mutandis applied to our Tribunal where instead we have a very specific Article 29, which is in a way worded in a forceful fashion. So therefore I would like you to comment on this issue. The second question is what you would say with regard to the only case, to the best of my knowledge, which relates to this issue, and which is more recent, namely the Godinez Cruz case, brought before the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. I have the text with me and I could read out the relevant passages. There, as you know, the court decided to ask the respondent, the Gvernment of Honduras, to provide the organisational chart showing the structure of Battalion 316 and its position within the armed forces of Honduras and set a deadline for submission of these documents. In response to that order, the Government of Honduras requested that the court receive the testimony of its Commandant in a closed hearing because of strict security reasons of the State of Honduras, and that hearing was held and the government of Honduras produced all the necessary documents relating to military matters. I wonder whether you could comment on this important precedent which in a way is more recent and more relevant to us than the Corfu Channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Okay, your Honour. With respect to the Corfu Channel case, in fact I think it is very applicable in this situation. One must keep in mind that in that case, the ICJ actually did have jurisdiction over both of the state parties who were involved there. Again, the International Tribunal lacks jurisdiction over States in our view, so that is one important -- the States were actually before the Corfu Channel court. In that circumstance, Article 49 gives the ICJ specific, express permission to ask States to turn over documentary evidence and indicates that if they do not, a note may be taken of it. Article 29, again, while it does speak in terms of requiring States to co-operate and requiring States to execute orders, does not provide express authority for the court to request States or even order States to turn over state papers. In some sense, the ICJ Statute, again because the ICJ has jurisdiction over States, or the parties before it are always States, has that express power and the International Tribunal does not, even in that case, where the court clearly did have that power, there was no sanction, the ICJ Statute does not provide for penal sanctions if a State declines to comply with the court's request and in that case, the court did not even take note, it did not hold it against Britain in deciding the case that it had not surrendered these documents which apparently had naval secrets involved in them. As to the other case, the Cortinez Cruz case, that case is also very significant, because there the State involved was not compelled to provide this information. States are always free to make a determination that "we will give the court our national security information". That is part of their sovereign right. Tomorrow, if the President of the US decided to do it, he could turn over to you all of the National Security Agencies' information on what went on in the former Yugoslavia. He could not be compelled, but he could do it, and that would be within his legal authority as President and it would be perfectly appropriate under international law. What the court did not do in the Cortinez Cruz case was seek to compel Honduras -- they made the request, Honduras came back and said "okay, but we would like, obviously, some precautions to be taken, in camera hearing"; the Court said "okay, we could do that" and the government then willingly provided the documents. States can always do that, they just cannot be compelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: May I add one brief point, your Honour? In general, it is our view that Article 29 and Tribunal statutory provisions have to be read and construed in a context of customary and treaty international law that has evolved for a long time, certainly since the advent of Italian city States in the 8th century. We believe that one of the inalienable attributes of sovereignty is indeed an absolutely prerogative to determine what its national security interests may be and how they can be best protected. It is not the case, as I think the Prosecution incorrectly suggests, that the only way to vindicate that right is to allow the Tribunal to fashion some procedures that, in the Prosecution's view, maybe even in the Tribunal's view, are sufficiently protective of that right. Again, as my colleague mentioned, while you can indeed surrender, on a case by case basis, or may be even by treaty, that power, you cannot imply its abdication from any language in Article 29, and it is that reason -- really looking at the Corfu Channel case, in addition to it being a specific precedent, is a very good statement of international law relative to the way the international tribunals look at their assertion of national security interests. Again, you have not asked in this instance, but just to briefly elaborate, it is completely different from a situation facing any domestic court, because if indeed the overall sovereign, of which the judicial branch is a part, concluded that courts shall have a final say in national security matters, so be it. In other States they can give this power to the legislative branch and in other States they can give it power to executive branch. These are purely power allocation issues and none of it, we would respectfully submit, is relevant here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I may comment on your remarks. First of all, I agree with you that customary international law should apply, and also our Statute must be interpreted within the framework of customary international law. However, whenever we find a provision which is clear, crystal clear, and whose wording does not provide for any exception, I wonder whether we should take into account customary international law. Here in Article 29(2) it is stated, and I quote: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or an order issued by the Trial Chamber." I do not see why one should read into this provision a particular qualification whereby documents which may raise military concerns may not be covered by this request for production of documents, but I wonder whether probably you could go into again two points which you insist upon in interpreting Article 29. Before our coffee break, counsel for Croatia pointed out that actually Article 29 -- this was also stated in one of the briefs from Croatia, Article 29 only addresses itself to States, not to the Tribunal. The second point, which is the basic one -- one of the basic tenets, of your interpretation of Article 29, is that, of course, 29 does not grant any jurisdiction to our Tribunal over States. As for the first point, I really am at loss to understand what you mean by saying that this Article only puts obligation upon States. Yes, by the same token it gives our Tribunal the power to act upon those obligations, because it is stated here, States shall comply with our orders, the orders of the Tribunal; this, of course, means the Tribunal is empowered to issue orders with which Member States of the international community are duty bound to comply. This is my first point. The second point, when you say you do not have, under Article 29, any jurisdiction over States, yes, of course, nobody would dare to say that we have the jurisdiction to prosecute and try States or state officials, except if state officials have committed war crimes, genocide and so on. But this does not imply that we do not need the co-operation of States for the collection of evidence. On the one side, we have jurisdiction, namely the power to prosecute and try individuals for alleged violations of international humanitarian law. On the other side, we have the authority and the power to request States to provide evidence or to co-operate with the Tribunal so that the Tribunal is put in a position to fulfil its mission, so therefore this notion of the absence of jurisdiction over States -- I do not think it leads anywhere as far as Article 29 is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, with respect, as to your first point, Article 29 creates an obligation for States. In our view, it does not create a corresponding jurisdiction or authority for the court, and if one contrasts Article 29, for example, with the Articles that do give the court its jurisdiction, Article 2: "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute." Article 3: "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute the persons violating laws or customs of war." The same language can be found in Articles 4, 5 and 6, perhaps even more apropos. "The International Tribunal shall have jurisdiction over natural persons." These are clear affirmative grants of authority to the Tribunal. By contrast, Article 29 does not include a grant of authority to the Tribunal. It requires States to do certain things. I am sure what your Honour would say is "at least by implication if States have to do these things then we get to do them", but I would submit, yes, the ability to do these things can be found elsewhere in the Statute, and that it is Article 29 that merely requires States to do them, to help you with requests for assistance and to execute orders. With respect to the jurisdiction, it is true that the court does not have substantive subject-matter, jurisdiction to try States. However, the court, I would submit, needs more than merely subject-matter jurisdiction in order to issue a binding order to someone. You need what is often expressed as "personal jurisdiction", you need legal authority over the entity in order to affect it with your orders. Indeed it would be comparable, say, to a court in Egypt issuing a order to a corporation or individual in Mexico who never had any contact with Egypt but for whatever reason may be of interest to the court. The court would have no power to bind that individual because they are beyond its jurisdiction. You need both subject-matter and personal jurisdiction before you can bind the individual or entity, and here, as the Court has itself accepted, it simply does not have personal jurisdiction over States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I mean, in the example you just made of Egypt and another country, say France, of course France would not be bound by any international treaty or international obligation, whereas we have here 29, so it is not a question of horizontal relationships between States, it is a vertical relationship. We have Article 29 which grants the Tribunal the power to bind all States of the international community, with you I do not want to -- in any case, just let me, as a footnote, add that the very presence of Croatia today here acting as a State proves that in a way the Tribunal has an ancillary or inherent jurisdiction over States, because otherwise you would not be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may answer that, I do not think -- Croatia has appeared to contest the court's jurisdiction, it has not agreed thereby or submitted itself to that jurisdiction by doing so. Yes, in domestic proceedings it can sometimes be the case that individuals who make the mistake, appear to contest jurisdiction, suddenly find themselves within the court's jurisdiction, but I would submit that for States, more than that is necessary, States can only be subjected to the jurisdiction of any Tribunal either by their own consent or by the Security Council. We do not argue. Clearly the Security Council could give you this power; our point is that we do not think they have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether there are any questions on this issue of national security. Yes, Judge Li?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: I would like to raise a question. If the power of determining the question of national security concerns belongs solely to the sovereign State, will there be any means to guarantee the right of this Tribunal to obtain the necessary documents for deciding the guilt or innocence of the accused? If there is such means, what is the means? Will you please state expressly? If there is no such means, is it not reasonable to admit the necessity of this Tribunal to determine whether national security concers are actually involved? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If indeed the Tribunal were to consider or to determine that particular documents of national security concern to a particular State were necessary, and in this case I think that is very far from being shown, convenient perhaps but not necessary, the Tribunal's recourse would be to go to the Security Council, to report the situation, indicating "we believe these documents exist and we believe that we need them", and ask the Security Council, using its Chapter VII powers, to impose the necessary sanctions, whether that be economic or political, or even military, against the State in question, to force it to divulge the documents; the Security Council clearly has the authority to do that. It is just that -- and indeed, if the court were to make such a report, that of itself we would not consider to be a sanction, that is simply the court going to the Security Council to ask for their help, enabling the court to be effective in a particular case and so yes, that would be the remedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may just add one thing, in fact there is an excellent example of a Security Council acting precisely in that situation, which involves Libyan sanctions. As all of you know, there are sanctions imposed on Libya largely for their failure to turn over individuals to Great Britain and the United States who are alleged to have been involved in Lockerbie, so the Security Council is quite used to coming to the aid of justice in this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, we can add that the Security Council is a specialised body whose name clearly indicates that it does, and it specialises in, security measures, it is a Security Council, so Security Council certainly will be perfectly competent and feel comfortable in deliberating whether certain refusal is justifiable, in the sense of the issue of national security, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions? We may now turn to the Prosecution. I wonder whether the Prosecutor is prepared -- we have 25 minutes to sum up the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may, I will try to make submissions that are somewhat responsive to the comments that were made this morning. In particular, I wish to note at the outset the admission that was made by the Republic of Croatia this morning by which it concedes that a State, including the Republic of Croatia, is the proper subject of a binding order for the production of documents. In light of that admission this morning, some of my other submissions may appear somewhat redundant, but considering that that appears to be a new position, certainly not reflected in the position taken by Croatia up to now, and not reflective of the position taken in their brief -- if I appear to be mistaken as to whether this admission was made, I will continue to address my submission accordingly, but I heard this morning this admission being made. I merely wish to state as an introduction the context in which this matter arose, it has already been alluded to by the appellant, in particular the fact that this was the first time in nearly four years of existence of the Tribunal that what I would call the "compliance mode" had to be resorted to. This Tribunal has functioned, certainly the office of the Prosecutor has functioned, with reasonable success by using up to now essentially the co-operation mode. Both methods are contemplated by Article 29 which imposes an obligation on States to co-operate and then, further, a separate obligation to comply with orders. The Prosecutor has always taken the position that it ought to exhaust the avenue of co-operation before resorting to these more intrusive measures. This has been done for the first time in this case, I submit, against a background of non-co-operation which is very well documented, was indeed reported to the Security Council, and is reflected in our briefs, paragraph 6 to 12. I will simply add to that that eight months after the original issuance of the subpoena, and some seven months after, at the request of the single Judge who was seized of the matter, we transferred our order for a subpoena to a request for assistance so as to explore once again the possibility of co-operation. We received four days ago a letter in which "a number of documents were said to have been found and collected", and at 9.15 this morning a small number of supplementary documents, not in compliance with the entire request in the request for assistance or the subpoena, were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. To this date, although the Republic of Croatia has made allegations with respect to the breadth of the subpoena, it has yet to identify with any specificity which of the documents it claims are the subject of national security concern. There is certainly a clear-cut case that it is not all of them, since a few have not been handed over and Croatia merely suggests that some may be the subject of that protective claim, and it has yet to identify which ones are alleged not to exist or not to be relevant. I also submit that this is not really within the ambit of the deliberations of this chamber to embark on a determination of the breadth of the subpoena. Our submissions are very straightforward. We assert that there is an express power in the Statute to issue orders to States. I will elaborate in a minute on that. We also assert that there is an express power in the Statute to issue orders to individuals. We further contend that in light of these two general propositions there is no exception in the Statute that would inure to the benefit of state officials, and finally we will contend that the national security privilege claim, if it can be made at all, cannot be an absolute bar, again in terms of the express language of the Statute, to the production of documents. If I may return and make some brief remarks with respect to the express power to issue orders to State, the language is, in my submission, absolutely clear in Article 29 and therefore the only issue before this chamber is whether or not there is any rule of interpretation or any principle of law which would require that this plain language be interpreted otherwise than in accordance with its unambiguous terms. Let me, if I may, address a few points that were made by counsel for the Republic of Croatia. The first one, if I understand it correctly, is that the language of Article 29 imposes an obligation on States to co-operate but does not otherwise empower the Tribunal to make the order. To the extent that I can understand the distinction, and I have to submit that the obligation certainly implies the power, but if one had to turn to a more specific ground of power, in my submission it is also clearly expressed in the Statute in Article 18(2) and 19(2). Article 18(2) speaks in the very language that counsel for Croatia referred to with respect to Articles 2 to 5 which uses language empowering the Tribunal; "the Tribunal shall have the power". Article 18(2) states: "The Prosecutor shall have the power to question suspects, victims and witnesses to collect evidence and to conduct on-site investigation." There is a specific ground of empowerment in the Prosecutor, which then is followed in Article 19(2) by the possibility, at the request of the Prosecutor, of an order of a Judge issuing for the proper conduct of the trial, so in my submission, if there was any concern raised that Article 29 is not in itself an article empowering the Tribunal to make the order but merely imposing an obligation on States, that should be entirely dispelled by tracing Article 29 in the proper context of these preceding sections. If I may address another issue that was advanced, as I understand it, by Croatia in its written briefs, both the first and the second one, but I understood it to have been abandoned this morning, in any event I will address it, and that is the statement that under Article 29(2) States cannot be the subject of the order. This, in my submission, carries a fundamental confusion between the primary jurisdiction of the Tribunal and its ancillary jurisdiction. By "ancillary jurisdiction", I do not mean "inherent" or "implied" powers. Ancillary jurisdiction can be implied or it may be express, but it is different than the primary jurisdiction to try persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia since 1991. The primary jurisdiction of the Tribunal is embodied essentially in Articles 1 to 9, but the Tribunal also has express ancillary jurisdiction -- which is embodied in many sections, I will refer to Articles 14, 15, 18 to 25, 27 and 28 and 29 -- which empower the Tribunal to do things that are necessary to the proper discharge of its mandate under its primary jurisdiction. Ancillary jurisdiction, in my submission, in this case is express. It is expressed in Article 29. Not all ancillary jurisdiction is so express. Some of it is properly inferred by the nature of the work of the Tribunal, and the enactment of Rule 108 bis in my submission is an example of a rule enacted under Article 15, but on the basis of a ground of empowerment which is merely implied. Article 25 of the Statute compels the Tribunal to hear appeals from persons convicted and from the Prosecutor. There is no Article compelling the Tribunal to hear appeals from States who may have an interest in the proceedings, but the plenary saw fit, under Article 15, to enact a Rule, in my submission as part of its ancillary, not express, but implied jurisdiction, to render justice in a fair manner to enact that provision. This is not our case. In our case, the jurisdiction -- ancillary not primary -- is express. It is expressed in Article 29. Therefore, the only question is whether this Article of the Statute should be read down in some fashion to exempt States from what appears to be their unambiguous duty. I would suggest that it ought not to be read contrary to its plain meaning, because its plain meaning is squarely consistent with the principle of efficacy upon which this Tribunal should proceed. If I may, I will now address the question of whether or not this express power to issue binding orders to States is also an express power to issue subpoenas to States. There are suggestions, certainly both by Croatia and in some of the amicus briefs, that "subpoena" implies the threat of a criminal sanction and therefore as a procedural instrument is unavailable against a State. Let me say at the outset that in my submission this is an incorrect characterisation of what a subpoena is in the many jurisdictions that have a common law origin and that use that procedure. Counsel for Croatia has just alluded this morning to the fact that, for instance, in the United States, and, I submit in many other jurisdictions, the penalty of contempt for failure to obey a subpoena is qualified as a civil contempt, not a criminal contempt, and it is certainly the case in many jurisdictions. I would submit that the amicus brief by the Max Planck Institute is very instructive in pointing out that both in civil law and in common law jurisdiction one ought to be very measured in using indiscriminately the concept of criminal sanctions, civil sanctions, administrative sanctions, or other forms of remedies. In my submission, the issuance of a subpoena, even if it were to lead to a finding of contempt, which, in my submission, is not an issue before the court, does not imply, even in common law jurisdictions, that it carries the threat of a criminal sanction. Indeed, I will submit that it does not even carry in reality, in the many jurisdictions where it is used, in reality the threat of any sanction at all. But more to the point, in my submission, it is inappropriate for this Tribunal, which has enacted Rule 89, in which it has stated very clearly that it is not bound by the rules of any particular system, it is inappropriate to assume that it has used language that would render the Rule it has enacted ultra vires. If indeed it is inappropriate to issue an order against the threat of sanction against a State, this Tribunal should not be presumed to have done so merely because it used a particular expression which may or may not contain that kind of connotation in some of the legal systems in which it is used. Rather, I would suggest that before this Tribunal, the proper Rule of interpretation that ought to be followed is the following: if language is capable of different interpretations, and I suggest that the word "subpoena" is wide open for interpretation, it should be interpreted in a manner that renders the provision valid within the competence of the enacting authority, while ensuring it is given the most effective meaning consistent with its object. In my submission, it would not be a proper method of interpretation for this Tribunal to interpret the word "subpoena" in a narrow fashion if only then to conclude that it was not within the competence of the plenary to enact it. A better rule of interpretation, and in my submission this is very consistent with international standards of interpretation -- I will refer to the Rights of Passage case in 1957, in the International Court of Justice at page 142, which states, in exactly the same spirit, and I quote: "It is a rule of interpretation that a text must, in principle, be interpreted as producing, and as intending to produce, effects in accordance with existing law and not in violation of it." So if the concern is that threats of criminal sanction, or indeed threats of sanctions at all, are inappropriate towards a State, I would submit that the word "subpoena" in Rule 54 of this Tribunal ought to be interpreted as not having that effect. There is again authority to support that proposition in the Max Planck Institute brief. In any event, and this will really sum up my position on this point, should the term "subpoena" be seen as inappropriate to state, even properly interpreted in accordance with the rule of interpretation that I submit is one that should be followed by this Tribunal, then in exercising its appellate powers under Article 25 of the Statute, which empowers the Appeal Chambers to reverse, uphold or revise a decision, it would be my submission that the proper outcome of this appeal should be to replace that word in the order under appeal by any suitable expression conveying that it is a binding order for the production of documents by Croatia under Rule 54 and under Article 29 of the Statute. In my submission, it matters not that the particular orders sought be upheld, although I continue to suggest that properly interpreted, there is absolutely nothing wrong with the use of that terminology. If I may, let me turn briefly to the question of the express power to issue orders to individuals. This power, in my submission, is express in the Statute and it is very clear that it has been taken for granted by the Trial Chamber below and by most of the parties who have been making submissions before this court, that there is indeed ancillary -- in my submission, express -- jurisdiction to issues orders compelling testimony and compelling the production of evidence directly against individuals without any restriction, except for the accused, of course, who is, under the Statute, the beneficiary of a specific exclusionary rule. Indeed, I would submit to the court that if individuals were not bound to produce evidence before the court, Article 21(4)(g), providing for the non-compelability of the accused, would have been unnecessary. Let me also, if I may, address what I understand, and again I may be mistaken, to be an argument which is put forward by Croatia which is that the power to compel evidence, testimonial or documentary, as I understand it, it is an argument that it is a power that can only be exercised against persons over which the Tribunal otherwise has jurisdiction. It would appear to suggest that ancillary jurisdiction must overlap with primary jurisdiction. In my submission, that is demonstrably absurd. It would suggest that the only persons who could be compelled to give evidence at a Tribunal are responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia since 1991, the very persons who are protected by their privilege against self-incrimination, and that clearly cannot be compelled to do so. So there is no question that the power which is vested in the Prosecutor in Article18 (2) and then can be the subject of court orders under Article 19, and then triggering the unambiguous obligation to comply on the part of States, is a power that could be exercised directly against individuals. Again, they are no reasons, no principle of interpretation or no rule of law, which would require a reading down or a narrowing of these powers, which not only are express but again, as demonstrated in the brief of the amicus, Max Planck, consistent with virtually every legal system, thereby illustrating the principle of efficacy. In that context my remarks with respect to State officials will be very brief. If there are no restrictions on the power to issue binding orders for the production of evidence against individuals, and no such restrictions against the power to issue binding orders for the production of evidence against States, there cannot be any possible legal foundation for the creation of an exception to benefit state officials. No such exemption exists in this Statute. The arguments that have been advanced in support of that kind of exception are based on an erroneous assumption of state immunity, which it is then suggested is passed down to state officials. If the State is not immune from the compelability of Article 29, there is no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker please slow down for the sake of the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: I think in this particular case the principle of efficacy. Slow down? Sorry. I believe that in this particular case, the necessity to have recourse to compulsory process against state officials has been very clearly illustrated in the case of the subpoena issued against the State of Bosnia, which concedes its obligation to comply and expresses its willingness to do so. The subpoena issued against a Minister of Defence, which you will recall is indeed an official of the Federation of Bosnia, over which the national state may or may not have the amount of control that one would otherwise assume a State has against its own Minister of Defence, and that Minister of Defence being not in compliance, so this -- if any example was required, we have one in this very case, of the necessity not to create an exception in favour of state officials that has no foundation either in the Statute or in any sound principle of law. I will briefly address the issue of national security interest. I point out that no such exception was created in the Statute, but the Prosecutor has conceded both below and before this chamber that in keeping with its implied ancillary jurisdiction, it would indeed be appropriate to create an exception against the rule of compelability to properly respect legitimate and well-founded national security interest claims, in the same way that other values which may not be expressly referred to in the Statute would deserve protection, such as personal privacy and other values that the Tribunal may wish to take into account. Under the existing rules, it is our submission that the Trial Chambers can scrutinise any specific claim of national security under Rule 89(B) and (D), and on that basis may then conclude that it would not be in the interest of justice to compel the production of any specific documents. I submit that under the existing rules there is ample provision to create -- to carve out an exception against what is otherwise the general compelability provision in the Statute based on the, in this case, merely implied ancillary power of the court. It would be my position that in light of the interest this question of national security has generated, it might be an area in which the Tribunal would see appropriate to legislate in a more specific manner, possibly after inviting further submissions by States, to carve out a methodology for addressing national security interest that will be responsive to the genuine claims of those States who ought to benefit from a presumption of good faith in light of the fact that they have no immediate interest in the case at bar and have a long history of co-operation on the one hand; and on the other hand carving a rule that would expose to much greater scrutiny States that have an immediate interest in many of the factual issues that are engaged in a case such as this one, and who have a long history of not co-operating with the Tribunal. This, of course, does not have to be decided within the ambit of this particular appeal. These are my submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. I think we may now adjourn until 2.30, and then probably we need a lot of time. We may go on until 6.00, with the agreement of the interpreters, and, if need be, resume tomorrow at 9.30. So for the time being, I propose that we adjourn and we will reconvene at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we start with questions for the Prosecutor and first of all questions about preliminary issues. I do not have any questions. I will ask Judge Li whether he would like to ask his question, but probably the Prosecutor is aware of the question Judge Li asked this morning on the notion of subpoena. Do you prefer Judge Li to repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: I think I have the question as to whether there was any particular rationale for the Prosecutor having chosen to request the issuance of a subpoena. As I understood the question, it was whether the Prosecutor was seeking any particular consequence by having used that form of order rather than another one. In case I have not understood the question properly, I should add that if the question is why a subpoena, rather than asking for mere co-operation, I think the record speaks for itself, that in our view we had exhausted the channels of co-operation. If the question is why a subpoena as opposed to any particular other form of order, the simple answer I suppose is that the subpoena is provided for in Rule 54 and understood as we submit is its proper interpretation, it appeared to us to have been the appropriate procedure by which to convey to the Republic of Croatia and to the Minister that it triggered their obligation to comply. There is, as I submitted this morning, no other consequence attached to the choosing of that particular form of order and both at the outset and today, we would be content with any variation of the order, as long as it would convey that it is a binding compulsory order within the meaning of that Rule and Article 2. Nothing else maybe turns on that choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Judge Li, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: The question I put this morning, there is another part. I would like to know whether the term "subpoena" can be understood as "binding order" instead of its original meaning, "under penalty in case of non-compliance", as used in common law systems. Now, if it can be understood so, please give the reasons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. In my submission, as properly interpreted in this international instrument, the word "subpoena" ought not to be given the narrow interpretation that it is given in some jurisdictions that have a history of common law tradition; that is, of carrying a threat of penalty. I should add that in many jurisdictions, the recourse to antiquated Latin expressions is now discouraged precisely for that purpose, because often the words continue to carry, for instance, a Latin origin that is no longer in keeping with the reality of the procedure. In my submission, in many common law jurisdictions that use the procedure of a subpoena to compel the attendance of a witness, in many instances, no penalty is imposed, although some may be contemplated in law, of a civil or administrative nature. No penalty is imposed to the witness, but compliance is required, for instance, by the assurance of what is sometimes called a "bench warrant", whereby if the witness does not appear in answer to a subpoena a further order is issued, requiring that the witness be brought before the court. When that is executed, no further penalties are sought against a witness, the subsequent procedure cures the default, so in my submission, whatever its origin and whatever its current understanding or practice in any common law jurisdiction, this court is not bound by any of those, and it ought to interpret its own rules in a manner that makes it intra vires and consistent with general principles of international law, so if the threat of sanction, particularly criminal sanction, is inappropriate against State, that expression should be read as not containing that threat within the context of these rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Let me explain my question again. You see, as Article 29(2) does not provide for subpoena, it only provides for request or an order to a sovereign state. Why did the OTP choose to apply for a subpoena instead of applying for a request or an order, as stipulated in that Article? I think there must be some special reason for choosing this expression, instead of choosing the expression used by Article 29(2). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The reason is that Rule 54 is the Rule that provides for a range of orders. That Rule, in our submission, is properly enacted under Article 15 and is reflective of a variety of orders that can be issued within the authority of Article 29. It provides that a Judge or a Trial Chamber may issue such orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants, transfer orders as may be necessary. Rightly or wrongly, we were of the view that a binding order for the production of a document was in fact a subpoena, and that it would therefore be more specific to use that expression, thereby conveying to the Republic of Croatia what the precise nature of the order was. As I indicated, should the form have been inappropriate, the essence remained that we were seeking an order within Article 29, binding on Croatia and on its Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Yes. May I explain my question again? A binding order may not be an order under penalty. I think these are two different things. A binding order is an order which should be complied with, but a subpoena is an order which, if not complied with, will be under penalty. That is, I think, the difference between these two things. Will you explain it to me, whether there is such a difference between a subpoena and a binding order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. In my submission, a subpoena, as understood by Rule 54, is not an order under threat of criminal sanction. That is absolutely clear. No one suggests that this Tribunal has criminal powers beyond that of its primary jurisdictions. Whether it is an order under threat of a civil penalty in appropriate cases, under threats of administrative sanction, or if issued against a State, under no threats whatsoever, I think is the very issue that has to be decided here. In my submission, that expression, although it has a Latin root that contains the word "pen" or "penalty", as properly interpreted by this court should be declared when this court stays the law, sur le droit, the court should state that this Latin word in this jurisdiction is not an order under threat of a penalty when issued against a State. As I said, in the alternative, it could revise the decision and issue a different sort of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Let me say a few words as to Rule 54. Of course it provides for subpoena, but it can also be interpreted as subpoena is only applicable to any individual, a private individual, while if the OTP wants a State to produce a document, it should not use the word "subpoena", but use the word "order", because in that Rule, in Rule 54, there is also the word "order", so the order can be also used instead of subpoena. I wonder whether you agree, whether you can agree that subpoena can only be used against private individuals while an order to a sovereign state must be used, an order, the expression "order", instead of "subpoena". That is my interpretation of this. Whether it is correct or not, I should like your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. In my submission, it is not appropriate in interpreting the Rules to give undue preference to one version over the other, particularly if by preferring the text of the English version, we end up creating an enormous difficulty that unduly restricts the proper application of the Rule. If this subpoena had been issued in French, it would have contained the word "assignation", and there could have been no possible argument that that word carried in itself the threat of a penalty. The French translation of "subpoena" by "assignation" is not unknown, I believe that is the practice in some bilingual countries like Canada, which, contrary to what Professor Pellet asserts, is very familiar with the concept of subpoena, even in its French-speaking part, so again I suggest there ought not to be undue weight attached to the fact that the English version of the Rules uses a Latin expression which, in my submission, in this Tribunal ought not to carry any preconceived procedural characteristic. It is for this court to decide what "subpoena" means and in my submission, it would not be appropriate to be unduly restrictive just because of the Latin origin of the word and to suggest it is inapplicable to States when we know under the Statute that States are bound by orders of exactly that characteristic, minus, arguably, any suggestion of a threat of criminal sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Stephen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I did have a question. It relates to the Statute and to two Articles that you yourself referred to, 18(2) and 19(2). 18(2) gives to the Prosecutor the power to question suspects, et cetera, and to collect evidence and to conduct onsite investigations. Then 19(2) deals with the situation after confirmation of an indictment, where the Judge may issue orders as may be required for the conduct of the trial. Do you see any distinction in terms of timing, as it were, between that and Article 29? In other words, can one use Article 29 and its compulsive power at a time when the trial has already begun to seek material which one might think properly falls under the heading of Article 18, investigation and preparation of indictment, namely the collection of evidence and conducting investigations? Does it not perhaps seem that the subpoena in this case is more appropriately involving itself in doing the very thing that Article 18(2) is concerned with, rather than seeking the production of specific documents under 29? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I suppose my preliminary observation would be that either way the duty to comply is triggered in part because Article 18(2) continues to provide that the Prosecutor may, as appropriate, seek the assistance of state authorities, and even though this certainly does not fall squarely to be decided in these proceedings, one could argue, and I submit that this is not for today to make that decision, that a request for assistance as contemplated by Article 29 is a reflection of the entitlement of the Prosecutor to seek assistance under Article 18 and, therefore, one would see a parallel in Article 29 between the duty to comply with the request of assistance under 18(2), or to comply with an order under Article 19(2). One can see a logical parallel. I do not think any of that falls to be decided here, but my overall submission on that point would be that the powers of the Prosecutor under Article 18 do not cease to exist and are not superceded by orders that can be made for the proper conduct of the trial. There is nothing in the Statute that indicates that the Prosecutor become functus in her investigative role when the proceedings have been launched. In fact, it would be contrary once again to prosecutorial practices anywhere. The Prosecutor is under a duty to continue to uncover any pertinent evidence, exculpatory or incriminating, until the very end of the case. So even if it could properly be suggested that the subpoena that was requested here was within the ambit of Article 18(2), I would suggest that it would still trigger an obligation to comply and would still have been validly issued even though the indictment had been confirmed, and indeed we are now mid trial and still awaiting compliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We may wish to take up this matter, because I think your question is also related to the contents of the order. Depending on whether the order is requested before or after the beginning of trial, the specificity of the order may change. Anyway, we will come back to this issue later on. I will try to make myself clear later on. I wonder whether there are any other questions on heading 1, "preliminary issues", or whether we can move on to the second class of questions, "orders to States". If you do not mind, I will start precisely with this question. Assuming that our Tribunal can issue a binding order to States for the production of documents, should this order be specific and identify some documents so as to avoid what we would normally call a "fishing expedition", so therefore now what Judge Stephen pointed out before is quite relevant. In particular, does this apply to orders requested by the Prosecutor and issued by a Trial Chamber after the beginning of a trial, where the need for the order to be specific, to identify some particular documents which are particularly relevant to the conduct of proceedings, becomes more imperative?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: If I may again put the matter in perspective, as I indicated at the outset, typically the Prosecutor will not seek orders either pre-indictment or post-indictment until the likelihood of useful co-operation has been exhausted, so not surprisingly, these orders may come rather late in the process, because one would want to exhaust all more amicable methods of exchange of information. It is our submission that although many documents are contemplated by the order here, they are material and relevant to essential ingredients of the offence, that we have the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt in the many aspects of this case, including any matter pertaining to the vast amount of circumstantial evidence that may be required to prove either the existence of an international armed conflict, particularly under standards set by the Trial Chamber in the Tadic decision; or alternatively to satisfy the Trial Chamber beyond a reasonable doubt on the issue of command responsibility. These are very unique elements of the crime, absolutely unique to this Tribunal, and their ambit as factual matters do not have a lot of equivalent in national jurisdictions. So if the scope of this subpoena may appear broad, we say that it is consistent with the factual elements that we need to prove, but in any event the question of the breadth of the subpoena, whether it was seeking information that was material, relevant, in existence, in the possession of the Republic of Croatia or the Minister, all these matters were matters to be debated between the parties and matters within the unique expertise of the Trial Chamber who can appreciate the relevance in light, as I indicated, of the very broad factual base of the elements of the crimes that are very unique.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a second question. In your view, in case of non-compliance by a State with a binding order issued by a Trial Chamber; what are the legal remedies available to our Tribunal? I say "remedies", not "sanctions".

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: I heard you, that was why I was immediately responsive to the question. We have never suggested that they were any other consequence, I will use that word, than the constat, the note of the failure to comply with the possibility now contemplated specifically in, I believe, Rule 7 bis of a report of that non-compliance to the Security Council. We have never suggested that there was any other consequences that would attach to the non-compliance by a State of an order, even if that order had the label "subpoena duces tecum" within Rule 54. We continue, obviously, to take that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other question on this particular point? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: May I raise another question? Suppose a State does not comply with a binding order of this Tribunal to produce documents, and this Tribunal reports to the Security Council, and the Security Council gives some sanction to that State; can the sanction be qualified as a punishment required by the non-compliance with the subpoena? Can the sanction of the Security Council be considered as a penalty of the sovereign state for the non-compliance with the requirement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Whether it is or it is not, in my submission it is no longer within the ambit of anything that this Tribunal would purport to be doing. The jurisdiction, the competence of the Tribunal would be exhausted by its reporting the non-compliance to the Security Council. Any further consequences, ranging from inaction on the part of the counsel to severe measures, I think would be completely outside the ambit of the Statute or anything that could be attributable to this Tribunal. That is why I say there are no further consequences, as long as we are remaining within the ambit of the authority of this institution, but to make that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other questions? So we can move on to item 3, "orders to state officials". There I have a couple of questions. Actually, I would like to raise a legal issue and a practical issue. Your position is very clear, so you, in a way, draw a sort of syllogism. States and individuals are not immune, they can be the subject of orders. State officials are individuals acting in their official capacity as state organs. Then the conclusion is: even state officials may be the subject or the addressees of a binding order. It is very clear. However, I wonder whether you take into account some principles of customary international law, particularly a rule which I think was very well summarised by the Supreme Court of Israel in the Eichmann case. If you do not mind, I will read out one small passage from that particular case. The court said, and I quote: "The theory of “Act of State” means that the act performed by a person as an organ of the State must be regarded as an act of the State alone. It follows that only the latter bears responsibility therefore and it also follows that another State has no right to punish the person who committed the act, save with the consent of the State whose mission he performed. Were it not so, the first State would be interfering in the internal affairs of the second, which is contrary to the conception of the equality of States based on their sovereignty." As you know, this is based on a practice of States going back to Canada, case of McLeod, when the British captain in Canada was arrested by the Americans and accused by the Americans of murder and arson, and the British authorities claimed that he was acting in his official capacity, so therefore the result was that Secretary of State Webster admitted that since he was acting not in his individual capacity but as a state organ, he could not be brought to court. This practice has gone on for many years up to the recent Rainbow Warrior case when France said "these two people who have blown up the Rainbow Warrior, they were acting as state agents, so New Zealand, you cannot bring to court those two people". All right, you may say this applies to interstate relations, so it is the famous principle of par in parem non habet imperium. It is the sovereign equality of States. What about an international court? My question is: judging from also the practice of international courts, it is clear that international courts have to comply with this customary principle of international law and I will say that even the Security Council, the supreme organ of the international community, has never issued any instructions or injunctions, I will say injunctions, to a Minister of Foreign Affairs of a particular country. The authorities of that country should behave this way, the leaders and so on, but never a particular organ, so therefore I think that even international courts and political organs have always taken into account this basic principle of customary international law. Therefore, you need to show that in our particular case we may disregard that particular customary rule of international law and address our orders to particular individuals acting in their official capacity, the Minister of Defence, the Minister of Foreign Affairs for country X, Y, Z. To do so, we need some sort of legislative authority. I know that you rely upon two provisions of our Statute, Article 7, paragraphs 2 and 4, and Article 18, paragraph 2. I wonder whether you could elaborate on this point, because I have, really, misgivings with your interpretation. So you can react to my observations, I would say Article 7, paragraph 2.4, deals with the criminal responsibility of individuals, the Head of State, Minister of Defence, who, according to the Prosecution, has committed war crimes or crimes against humanity; of course he cannot rely upon the rule of customary international law which I have just mentioned. This was, among other things, pointed out by the Supreme Court of Israel in the Eichmann case, because the only exception under customary international law to the so-called theory of "Act of State" is precisely the case of war crimes, crimes against humanity or genocide, so therefore, I wonder whether Article 7, paragraphs 2 and 4 may be of relevance. As for Article 18, paragraph 2, one may object to your interpretation, which is based on the second sentence: "In carrying out these tasks, the Prosecutor may, as appropriate, seek the assistance of the state authorities concerned." Your interpretation is based on this particular sentence and you say "it is clear in this case, therefore, the Prosecutor can address itself to particular state organs, say Minister of Justice, Minister of Defence, and seek the assistance of that particular Minister; that means that the whole Tribunal has such a power, and upon application the Tribunal can issue an order to a particular Minister". But I would point out that here if you compare the two sentences it is clear that in the first sentence the Prosecutor "shall have the power to question suspects", "shall have the power". Then the second provision is that the Prosecutor "may, as appropriate, seek the assistance of the state authorities concerned". That means that in the first case you have the power to question, and you have a compelling power, you may question people and collect evidence and people cannot refuse to co-operate, whereas in the second case the Prosecutor may seek the assistance -- in French it is even clearer, "solliciter le concours des authorités". That means "are you prepared to co-operate?", so you do not have any binding power. A fortiori, we do not have -- the problem with the whole Tribunal is that we would not have such a binding power. Therefore I would like you to respond, to address my sort of doubts or misgivings about the interpretation of these two particular provisions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Let me say at the outset that I am not resting the argument on any of these two provisions, either taken alone or together, but on first principles. But let me first address why these two provisions were referred to. With respect to Article 7, subsection 2, the argument was advanced simply in response to the argument advanced by Croatia, which operated this confusion of ancillary jurisdiction and primary jurisdiction. Croatia was advancing the argument that there could not be possibly any power to compel evidence from States since they were not the subject of the primary jurisdiction of the Tribunal. We reject that submission, but to the extent that it could possibly have some foundation, we refer to Article 7(2) to say, certainly in the case of individuals and more particularly state officials, that argument squarely falls down. I am not suggesting that in itself 7(2) is the foundation of any entitlement to compel the production of evidence from state officials; indeed, I reject altogether any suggestion that the power to compel evidence is tied to the power to convict a person, so it is very much an alternative submission that was advanced to respond to the framework of analysis that was being put forward, but I am not suggesting for one minute that the Tribunal's entitlement to seek the co-operation and indeed the compliance of state officials is based on its capacity to punish them should they commit offences within our jurisdiction. The same is true of Article 18(2). This was advanced and I advance it as an example of the Tribunal's entitlement to address state officials. It carries no more weight than that. It is an illustration of the fact that the Statute contemplates instances in which the Tribunal may speak not just to a State but to a state authority. It carries no more weight. What I say is the entitlement of the Tribunal to compel the production of evidence, testimonial or documentary from a state official is based on first principles and not on the language of any of these particular sections, and the first principle is that whatever privileged position a state official may be in in international law, he cannot be in a better position than the State is. If we are correct on the fundamental assumption that I say is absolutely plain under Article 29, that States are the proper subject of binding orders for the production of evidence, so are their officials, unless there is something to indicate otherwise. They cannot be in any preferred position, put another way, they cannot claim the blanket protection of any State immunity beyond the immunity that the State itself possesses. In this case, we say there is no state immunity from the compulsory production of testimonial or documentary evidence and therefore state officials cannot claim any preferential position there, particularly hence the syllogism, in a framework where all other individuals are in no preferred position. For instance, there is no basis whatsoever to distinguish between the moral or legal responsibility of, for instance, the head of a private enterprise, a bank or a hospital, who may be compelled to produce documents to this Tribunal against the wishes of his government, and under this analysis would have no protection or immunity, as opposed to a government official acting on behalf of the very government that we say has the equal obligation to produce the materials, so my argument is very much based on first principle and on the global interpretation and does not rest on any of the two provisions that were used in a subsidiary fashion to support, but certainly not to anchor the main argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that you have slightly changed your attitude, because in your reply on page 2, at (ii), a reference is made to these provisions, but it is not of relevance. If what you say is correct -- let me move on to my practical question. A state official is the addressee of a binding order of our Tribunal, and he has been instructed by his government to disregard the order of our Tribunal. What would be the practical purpose of summoning this state official? Why should we ask him to come over and explain why he is not complying with this order if he simply claims that since his authorities have decided that he should not comply with a particular order, there will be no compliance? Our interlocutor in a way is always the State, so I do not see the practical purpose of involving the particular state official. As long as the state official is acting as a tool in the hands, as a sort of instrumentality in the hands of a State. This morning, we made the example of a state official who, in disregard of the instructions of his government authority, decides not to produce the document; in this case, I would say he should be downgraded to a sort of individual acting in his private capacity. But if the individual is complying with the instructions of his government -- as I say, I do not see the practical purpose of again involving this particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: In my submission, the practical purpose may also be lost in many instances in which valid binding orders will be issued against States who will not comply and who may or may not be made to comply outside the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, so the fact that validly-issued binding orders may not in any particular case yield any practical result in the short run, I think that does not detract from the fact that the order should be available. In fact, there may be benefit in other circumstances. It should not follow that because in some cases no practical purposes may be achieved, that we should abandon a technique that is otherwise lawful and available. That I think is clearly illustrated by the fact that there are many instances in which it may yield a practical result to be able to issue the order directly against a state official. I think the example that we have before us of the willingness of Bosnia to comply, but the unwillingness of the Minister of Defence of one of its entities, over which it may or may not have a community of interest that we would otherwise assume between a government and its Minister of Defence, I think is an example, frankly, that would have been difficult to imagine or to draw, and yet we have it exactly before us. We operate, and I think that we will continue to operate, in circumstances where governmental structure post-conflict may not be as solidly established as we would normally expect and we may encounter again in the pursuit of this kind of mandate situations where there may be a real impotence on the part of a government to make an official, either of a sub-entity or someone who is de facto control of documentary evidence, we may encounter situations where that government may have enormous difficulty ensuring compliance, even when it is willing to do so. Essentially my submission is that we ought to examine the availability of the order regardless of whether we anticipate an immediate benefit in applying it. If this order is validly and squarely within the competence of this Tribunal, we ought not to walk away from it in fear that in many cases it may add little. For instance, if a government official would merely obey the order to the extent of attending before the Tribunal and stating that the reason he is not producing documents is because he is under orders from his government to do so, I believe we would have achieved a considerable amount of progress, even though at the end we would still not have compliance with the order. So in my submission, it is not the practical reality that in many cases, in some cases, it may not appear to yield a practical result, that we should stay away from acknowledging that it is a perfectly legitimate and legal tool for this Tribunal to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to be a bit stubborn, to come back again to this issue, but I think it is a crucial issue which involves the question of the authority of our Tribunal. Let me pick up one of your arguments. First of all, you said "if the order had not been sent to the Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina we would not have achieved this practical result". Why? If the order had been sent, a binding order to the central authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and there the situation is really exceptionally unique, because normally state organs do comply with the orders of their national authorities -- but if the order had been sent only to the central authorities, the central authorities would of course have requested the particular Minister to comply with the order. The Minister would have refused and then the authorities would have reported to us, "sorry, we cannot do anything because the relevant state official who has the documents refuses to comply with these documents"; at that stage only I think, this is my submission, could we have regarded that particular state official not as a state organ, because he is not acting as a tool in the hands of the state apparatus, but as somebody who is following his own policy, as a sort of individual? At that stage, he could be the addressee of a binding order, because he then would have to come over and deliver those documents. So I do not see any difference, as far as the practical result is concerned. As for what you said concerning the advantage of having a state official coming here and saying "I am sorry, I cannot produce these documents because my Prime Minister said to me I cannot do so", I do not see any major advantage vis-a-vis the situation whereby a written note is sent by the Prime Minister or the official to our Tribunal saying, "sorry, our authorities refuse or decline to comply with your request". On the other hand, and here this is a practical point, if we have to resort to a legal remedy, the legal remedy will always be, and I think we agree on this point, at least you and I, reporting to the Security Council, we would not report to the Security Council on non-compliance with this order by a state official. This would be always the State, so in any case -- so therefore what is the point of having here a Foreign Minister or Minister of Defence if in any case our legal remedy would have as its main object the State as such, non-compliance by State with Article 29, whatever the position of the state official, Therefore, with all due respect, I fail to see the importance of involving state officials, the more so because I cannot see any major argument supporting the disregard of a basic principle of customary international law, what the Eichmann case called the "Act of State", the "Act of State Doctrine", which is acted upon by all States, All States and international organs are very keen on this so-called "Act of State Doctrine" because, as I say, it is a sort of protection of national sovereignty, the idea being that international organs or other countries have nothing to do, have no say whatsoever on the internal organisation of a particular sovereign State. They cannot interfere, cannot say "you are the Minister in charge of this matter and I asked you to do this and that", it is essentially for the authorities to decide how to behave for the purpose of respecting international obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: This, in my submission, though, would have very little convincing power in a situation where the State itself is already obligated to do the very thing we are asking of its official. It is one thing to respect a state's sovereignty and to entitle a State, in a sense, to blanket its officials with the same sovereignty. This is not the case here. If we are correct and we have already established that the State itself can be bound by the order, it is extremely difficult to sustain the proposition that it can then use the sovereignty which it cannot even use to protect itself to suggest that the State can then use it to protect its officials. In my submission, it is a clearly distinguishable case in which, as I said before, if we have jurisdiction over all persons, not just persons that are the subject of the primary jurisdiction, and over all States, assuming the order is validly issued, there becomes no principle of international law or logic that justifies the carving of this exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions on this issue? Can we have move on to the fourth item, orders to individuals. If I may start with a practical question. I think there is agreement on the idea that, of course, in any case, binding orders for the production of documents or summonses to individuals so that they may testify before our Tribunal may be addressed to individuals under the jurisdiction of sovereign states if, of course, those individuals are of some relevance, whatever they say -- what they may say or the documents they may possess are of some relevance to our proceedings. All right. My practical question is as follows: how do you envisage, and what is your practice, probably, in the OTP -- do you address those particular orders to individuals, or do you go through the national authorities? We know that say some States, Finland, Italy, France, Norway, Spain, Germany, Switzerland, they, in their implementing legislation, they state that any request for judicial assistance -- this is the expression used -- "must be sent to some authority in the capital city of those countries, or to a particular -- Court of Appeal or Supreme Court or the chief prosecutor" and so on, and they may then implement our orders. My practical question is whether you envisage the possibility of addressing a subpoena -- in this case we could call it "subpoena" -- directly to the individual, or whether you feel that one should go through the national channels, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: To this point, and consistent with what I have said at the outset of this case, the question has never really arisen. We have followed essentially on the co-operation mode the lead that was presented to us by the different countries with which we have dealings. Some, for instance, in the case of lay witnesses, non-government officials, non-military witnesses, are quite content to permit us to deal directly with the witnesses, and frankly in most cases it is not necessary to use the compulsion of a court order, the witness will voluntarily accept the invitation to come to testify. In other cases, we have agreed, again in the spirit of co-operation, and because it yields the acceptable result, to send all requests through government co-operation office, so the practice that we have followed so far is that we will do it essentially on a co-operative basis, whichever way the State prefers. Having said that, the ultimate position though is that in my submission, under operative paragraph 4 of Resolution 827, the duty to comply, the duty to co-operate and the duty to comply, is a duty that each State must accommodate and if any domestic legislation was either intended or had the effect in fact to bar co-operation or compliance, we would assert, as we have done in the case of arrest warrants consistently, that the States have an obligation to comply and cannot rely on any of their domestic legislation, including their constitution, for a failure to do so. So if, theoretically, state-enacted legislation barring access to its citizens for the purpose of compelling them to give evidence, we would say that in international law that legislation is invalid. We would then assert the Tribunal's entitlement to reach out directly to the individual by issuing an order to that effect, presumably permitting the individual to obey the higher order of international law, even in disobedience to his own domestic law. I think it would be counterproductive to suggest that we are at the mercy of using a state machinery when its citizens may be more willing than their government to discharge their obligations to this institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you say, in this case you have just now described, in a case of non-compliance by a State with such an order or subpoena, would you then notify, address directly the subpoena or the order to the individual concerned, say a French or Italian citizen who refuses to come here as a witness, to testify as a witness, or to produce documents. If the relevant national authorities refuse to enforce the order issued by the Trial Chamber, would you then -- how can he be made to have cognisance of this particular order -- say one could send it by mail to this person, the particular subpoena? Because normally in our countries a judicial officer normally goes to the person who has been subpoenaed, to notify the particular order. I wonder whether we could use our own investigators for the purpose of notification and I wonder whether sovereign countries will accept such a sort of interference with their sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: In my submission, the obligation on the States that is imposed by the resolution to co-operate and comply with the tribunals and enforce its orders, including for the production of evidence, requires the States to facilitate our access to all witnesses including lay witnesses. There is no question that if the witness and the State are both non-responsive we are again in the situation unfortunately of having very little practical recourse, but I would submit that if the witness -- there are reasons to believe that the witness would be willing to comply but the State, either because of its legislation or its attitude, if it has not enacted legislation, is not willing to assist, that we would have every entitlement to reach out directly, by mail might be the preferable, more prudent course than sending members of our personnel to an unfriendly territory for that simple purpose, but that is just modernality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: One final question. In case of non-compliance by individuals and by States, of course, against the State one has a legal remedy: reporting to the Security Council, but what about individuals? Do you think one could use the contempt proceedings and then, of course, resort to proceedings in absentia by using the general notion of contempt?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: In my submission, this issue is hypothetical in the extreme, there is no factual basis to analyse it and furthermore, it requires an analysis of not only the wisdom of this kind of practice but of whether or not it is even open under the current rules. What my submission would be is that if an order was issued requiring the attendance of a lay witness, non-government official, and the witness was not forthcoming, I would submit that the Prosecutor or the Defence or the bench on its own motion may then want to issue an order to the State concerned to actually apprehend the witness and bring that person to the Tribunal. In most cases, if that procedure were to be successful in my opinion there would be no point, either in law or in fact, in pursuing any issue of disobedience to the original order to appear. The matter would be rendered moot by the fact that we would have obtained what was desired, which is either the documents or the testimonial evidence of the witness. In my opinion, it is hypothetical and speculative in the extreme to contemplate a trial in absentia on a charge of contempt, particularly considering our limited resources, which at the end of the day would yield nothing more than the possibility of issuing that kind of compulsory process. My submission would be that the non-compliance with an order to appear by a person should be followed by any person -- and, in my submission, this would include a state official -- should be followed by an order to the State to produce the official, in assistance to the Tribunal and that failure, whether it is by a government with respect to a state official or a lay witness, would then become the additional failure of the State to be visited upon it in the usual fashion of reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on to our last item, "national security concerns". I should stop asking questions. I wonder whether you have any questions on national security concerns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Judge Li.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: May I raise this question? Do you agree with the proposition that the power of determining the question of national security concerns belongs solely to the sovereign state; or do you think it reasonable and proper that the power of determining this question should belong to this Tribunal, instead of belonging to the sovereign state concerned. Will you please state your position? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you. My position is that the determination of a claim that evidence that is otherwise compulsory should not be produced because of concerns of national security, that is an issue that is for the determination of this Tribunal. I say that first because the Statute itself, and the Rules, do not provide for any exemption from the duty to produce evidence, a duty that I say exists on the part of States. The Statute provides for no exception and that if one is to be determined it ought to be determined by this Tribunal, weighing on the one hand the interest of international criminal justice in coming to a fair and accurate disposition of the case against the legitimate and substantiated concerns of a State that exposure of the information that is sought could jeopardise its national interests.
