I would submit that, as was illustrated in the case that the President referred to earlier, in the same way that we do for witness protection, there are many protective measures that are available to an institution like this one to meet the genuine national security interests of many States, and I would also submit that if appropriate the Tribunal could devise a rule of the utmost deference to national security interests, particularly when a claim on its face would appear to have a very strong legitimate basis if it was coming from a State that had a long history of co-operation with the Tribunal, that had no observable interest in the outcome of the case, and when, on its face, the materials sought were of a highly sensitive nature. I can imagine cases where the Tribunal would want to offer the utmost deference to the claim. It would range from cases such as this one, where I would suggest that the claim became unsubstantiated and unparticularised, that it has been advanced here ought to be subjected to the most intense level of scrutiny because of all the circumstances of this case, so my brief answer is that it would be utterly inconsistent with the express provisions of the Statute and the Rules and with fair principles of international criminal law to give an absolute blanket privilege to States to defeat their obligation to produce evidence by a mere assertion of a national security interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: May I raise another question? What safeguards do you think it necessary for this Tribunal to provide for in order to accommodate the national security concerns of a sovereign state in respect of the production of documents? I mean, what safeguards should be provided for? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: In this particular case, my submission would be that it would be incumbent on the Republic of Croatia to solicit protective measures such as in camera hearing and so on. What I would not advocate at this point, without a factual specific basis to analyse the issue, is any particular safeguard. In general terms, though, my submission would be that the safeguards should be well developed and should be explicit and should be reflected in a Rule that could be enacted, as I said, as part of the implicit, implied ancillary power of the Tribunal, there being nothing in the Statute on that, a Rule that could be developed after consultation with States, all of whom have a long history of handling these difficult situations of the conflict between international security concerns and the proper functioning of their criminal justice system. Once again, I may turn to the Max Planck Institute brief, which does a summary but quite thorough review of the issue, and I think supports very much that position. As to what general safeguards would be appropriate, my submission is that States should be consulted, but I would, as I indicated before, contemplate that there ought to be a wide range of measures put in place and put in place expressly, but there is no suggestion that this case could not be adjudicated in the absence of this framework. In my submission, under Rule 89(B) and (D), the court is very capable of making that determination in this case, and I say this is a case that deserves the least level of deference to the claim until it is better substantiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any more questions? I have two small questions. In preparing for these hearings, I came across an interesting case decided upon by the House of Lords in 1984. It is Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service. There Lord Frasier said, and I quote, this is a sentence which is so puzzling to me: "The decision on whether the requirements of national security outweigh the duty of fairness in any particular case is for the government and not for the courts. The government alone has access to the necessary information and in any event the judicial process is unsuitable for reaching decisions of national security." "The judicial process is unsuitable for reaching decisions of national security"; do you think that one is in a way warranted in disregarding this important statement by Lord Frasier based on the overriding authority of our Tribunal, and because of Article 29? This is one question. If you do not mind, I apologise, but I think the Australian legislation, implementing legislation, includes a provision whereby in case of military matters and so on, Australia would, by law, refuse to provide any documents, so it is in the Australian law implementing our Statute. There again, what would you say, that we should disregard such a piece of legislation because of the well-known principle whereby international law prevails upon national legislation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: I will start with the last question, because I think the answer is in fact straightforward, that depending on the ultimate decision of this court, but if the decision of this court was that the national security interest cannot be asserted as an absolute bar to the duty to produce evidence, any domestic law to the contrary would have to yield. I say that on the basis of the Statute as it exists now, there is no foundation. The Security Council has not seen fit to reserve that particular interest under an exclusionary rule, and yet it has dealt with other exclusionary rules, the solicitor/client privilege and the privilege against self-incrimination, and one that is equally well-known in many legal systems is the national security privilege, and the Security Council has not seen fit at this stage to give it its protection. I still submit that it is an appropriate interest to be protected, but at this stage it certainly could not be given, in my submission, as an absolute bar by this Tribunal absent a clear position by the Security Council in creating the Tribunal in the Statute, and any national law to the contrary would have to yield. As for the case that you have referred to, I regret that I am not in a position to give you a full expose of English law on this matter. In my recollection, starting with Conway and Rimmer, there has been a great revolution in English law, as with many other common law countries, starting from an absolute privilege moving towards the more modern approach of a fine-tuned balancing of interest, which is, I think, the preferred approach, so I could not assert here today that the case that you have referred to is actually an accurate up to date statement of the law of England. In fact, I am inclined to believe that it is not in part on the basis of the information that is provided to us in the Max Planck brief. If I may just address that particular point, at page 15 and 16, in the middle of the top paragraph at page 15, reviewing the question of the doctrine of public interest immunity -- this is in paragraph 43 of the Max Planck Institute brief: "The review of the applicable domestic law in England and Wales leads the learned authors of the brief to conclude that the final assessment lies with the court" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down for the sake of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: -- and then a reference to later decisions: "However, the House of Lords made clear that even in the case of" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker please slow down, it is too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: -- "claims, and on rare occasions to require their disclosure."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: There are some jurisdictions, there is no question, where the claim of national security is an absolute bar, and where the courts have no supervisory power. I believe that the majority of jurisdictions reviewed is the other way, and I say in this jurisdiction, particularly in light of an absence of direction in that respect from the Security Council in creating the Statute, there is no reason to conclude that there is a absolute national security privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to perhaps a Rule which you are fairly familiar with? I see that Rule 66(C) contains a provision which might confront you in circumstances where disclosure affects the public interest which might involve national security. How would you handle such a situation if you come across it? This is disclosure by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: This I think is an indication of the fact that such information ought to be offered the highest level of protection, particularly, and this is a good example I think, of the Tribunal exercising exactly that kind of discretion in relieving the Prosecution from some disclosure obligation that would unduly jeopardise national security interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: On the other hand, could not the Defence or any third party rely on the same provision for national security?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: That Rule deals only with withholding of information from pre-trial disclosure. It is not a rule that then bars the use of evidence at trial. Presumably if the Prosecution could obtain an order under Rule 66(C), if the need arose further to tender this evidence at trial, the Prosecution would then seek similar protective measures at trial, such as requesting that the evidence tendered be offered in camera, that the documents be received by the Tribunal under seal, for instance, would seek any measures to try to protect this interest, but this in no way indicates that a national security interest overrides the fact-finding process to such an extent that it ought not to be tendered during the course of the trial. It is merely a pre-trial protective measure, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am only thinking aloud. Perhaps it might assist the Defence or someone else who still has the same interest in protecting whatever is the national security interest, especially as in this case or any other case of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Stephen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am just curious about the practical effect of your submission. Let us assume that Croatia says that the hundreds, perhaps thousands of documents that are referred to in very wide terms in the present document, the present subpoena, do indeed all relate to its national security and are still relevant to that. Would you contemplate that at this stage there be an investigation, document by document, by this Tribunal of that claim which might take months, perhaps years, while the trial is presumably adjourned for that purpose? Is that the way it would work?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: The one thing that I think ought not to be contemplated is that Croatia could decline the production of documents by merely asserting that all the documents requested pertain to its national security interests. So between the evil of lenity scrutiny and the evil of not getting the evidence at all, much as I hate to admit it, I would have to say we would have to embark on some kind of analysis. It seems to me that the threshold is for the person who is under the obligation to produce to assert, specify and substantiate the claim, for instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, what do you mean by "substantiate"? I understand "assert" and I suspect there might be such an assertion. What do you mean by "substantiate" before the process would come into operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: If I may give an extreme example, it seems to me that some claims could be rejected on their face, without examining the document, on the simple basis that within the meaning of the protection, the claim would not constitute a bona fide legitimate claim of national security interest that ought to be sustained by this Tribunal. For example, if the Republic of Croatia objected to the production of the documents we are seeking, on the basis that they would tend to show its participation in an international armed conflict and were asserting that such demonstration would be contrary to its national interest, I would say on its face the claim ought to be rejected. You would not even have to examine the document, you would say -- it is not a subjective determination of what is or is not in the national security interest of a State. In the context of what this enterprise is all about, I think many claims would not need to be substantiated within the documents but would have no merits on their face. Others, I think, could also be accepted by the Tribunal again without a great deal of scrutiny of the documents. For example, if the documents sought again on their face related to contemporaneous -- not historical but contemporaneous -- military equipment or matters of some sensitivity where the Prosecutor would have difficulty showing the probative value that it would have to the historical events under scrutiny; again, without examining the documents, the court could reject the claim. So I think one can contemplate disposing of many of these matters first by examining the claim without examining the documents. In the case where they would be an ongoing battle about the content of the documents, again I would say that should it be in the course of an ongoing trial, as unfortunately we are now with this particular issue, that should have been resolved by a substantiated claim much earlier in my submission. Maybe then the only recourse to expedite matters would be for the Trial Chamber or one of its delegated members to proceed very expeditiously to a review of a sample of the documents. Unfortunately, I believe that the determination would have to be done, but in my submission, in many cases it could be done by pressing what is the interest that is being asserted and giving it a real factual foundation without the need for that kind of detailed scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any other questions? No. Thank you very much indeed. Now we, before we break for coffee, I will turn to the Defence counsel for General Blaskic to ask whether they intend to make any statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have a few comments, Mr. President, perhaps 10 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Defence, Mr. President and your Honours, has four areas of comment. One goes to the process, two go to the factual context within which this debate is going on and the fourth is a legal point. First as to the process. We urge the appellate chamber to act on this matter as quickly as it possibly can, and that is because we are engaged in a trial right now, General Blaskic's future lies in the balance, we fear that this issue could be the basis on which the Prosecution may seek delay in the case at some point in the future. We simply note that the Prosecution waited some 14 months after the indictment in this case to even seek the subpoena, so we hope that the process moves forward quickly and that we will not see further delays in our trial and in our case due to this issue, despite its importance. We also believe it would facilitate the process and a speedy resolution of these issues if, after the Chamber Rules, it remands the issue not to Trial Chamber II but to Trial Chamber I, where we believe it should have been brought in the first instance. It is very difficult, we believe, for Trial Chamber I to manage the case, manage the trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Trial Chamber II.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge Jorda and Trial Chamber I. If I mis-spoke, I mis-spoke. It is difficult for Trial Chamber I to effectively exercise its case management responsibilities while this matter is in front of a different Trial Chamber, setting its own schedule, in essence having a life of its own, so we strongly urge the appellate chamber to do so, and we note that all of the matters relating to orders for documents and so forth which the Defence has sought or is seeking have been brought directly to Trial Chamber I. Now to our first factual point. There are certain representations in the reply brief of the Prosecutor's office, as well as in madam Prosecutor's comments here today, that suggest that the Prosecution has and is exercising an obligation to seek exculpatory material as to the accused in this case. In essence, the Prosecutor suggests that they have, either under the rules, or they have voluntarily accepted the role of an investigative magistrate, something akin to that function. We do not believe that is the case, either under the Rules, or the Statute, or in terms of the actual practice in this case, and this is important as the court thinks about these issues, because the Defence is very critically involved in our own investigation of this case, we have been since the beginning of this case, and the very powers and authorities that are being discussed are not only just as important but we maintain more important in terms of the basic rights of the accused. So, we dispute that the Prosecution has any function in terms of investigating for exculpatory information. It is true where they find it they must turn it over under Rule 68, but they do not have an obligation to seek it out, they are not, in our belief, and in fact if you look at their subpoena to the Republic of Croatia, you see for example in paragraph 10, they seek all records of assistance to the HVO, presumably in an attempt to prove an international armed conflict. Nowhere do they seek any evidence of assistance to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would tend to show a lack of international armed conflict. We simply wish to underscore that the Defence has its own compelling and legitimate investigative needs so the very procedures which are being discussed are critical to the accused's interests and the Defence's ability to investigate. Indeed, in the subpoena duces tecum to the Republic of Croatia, there are lengthy lists of military units, for example on pages 3, 4 and 5, and we note that with respect to the discovery material we have seen in the case there is no basis to believe any of these units were in Central Bosnia at any relevant point in time to the charges herein. Our second factual point, Mr. President, deals with not subpoena, because we have never caused a subpoena to issue on our behalf, but order compelling the production of documents which we obtained through the Tribunal and Judge Jan issued in April of this year to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We sought that order on 2nd February 1997 and it was issued in April. I think I should say a word about it, so that while the court is considering this dispute it has in a general sense in mind what is going on on the other half of the battle ground here. We sought by order records of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning their military forces in the Lasva Valley during relevant time periods to this case. The relevance of that information is simply that while the Prosecution in a general sense maintains that during the conflicts, the periods of conflict in this matter, there were no army of BiH -- that is Bosnia-Herzegovina -- troops in the Lasva Valley; thus if that is true it was a conflict between soldiers and civilians on the Croat side and simply civilians on the side of the Bosnians. If that is not true, if there were Bosnian soldiers in the area, then necessarily these conflicts involved to a certain extent conflicts between soldiers, not simply the killing of civilians by soldiers. So, we sought those records by order, and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina replied with the production of certain documents which unfortunately did not pertain to military activities, they pertained, for example, to permits for aid convoys, permits for persons to enter military headquarters, but not to the operational matters, what units were where and what were they doing during time periods relevant to the case. On August 1st, we filed a motion for a deposition of the custodian of these records and then, on August 19th, we filed a motion for an order to show cause why Bosnia-Herzegovina should not be found to be non-compliant with Judge Jan's order. Having said that they did not have any more records, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina then filed a letter some six weeks ago with the Tribunal, stating that they believed they had discovered additional documents and asked for another 30 days to produce them. Those 30 days expired some two weeks ago and no additional documents have been produced. To my fourth and last point, which is a legal point, and that is we have had a very limited role in the legal propositions being disputed and discussed in this matter. Our general position has been that the Defence has a right to at least the same process and the same access to proof that the Prosecutor does. But in fact, I wish to note and suggest that in the opinion that you render, you consider reflecting, if only in passing, on the following proposition, that there may well be an asymmetry between the Prosecutor's right to have access to these compulsory powers and those of the accused. Why might that be, if you will bear with me for a moment? First, as to specificity, how specific must an order be? While the Prosecutor has agreements with many governments, access to the records of many international organisations, you have heard the Prosecutor describe how their investigative and other efforts have largely been voluntary on the part of other parties and individuals. That has been their situation. On the part of the Defence, it has been far from it. When we knock on doors, more often they are closed than opened, and that is true of governments, it is true of non-governmental organisations and it is sometimes true of individuals. So to say to the Defence that we cannot obtain an order compelling the production of a document unless we can specify the title, the date, the author of the document, would be to say that we have no power to investigate such matters because we have not already seen them, "you have not already seen the document, Mr. Nobilo, so you cannot get an order compelling its production". To do so would in effect preclude us from conducting a thorough investigation as we are duty bound to do. A second example of the asymmetry may well exist as to these legal rights and processes, and that is in the national security realm. We have seen in our case that the Prosecutor has been able to obtain national security information from one or more governments because the Prosecutor has Rule 70 to rely upon. Rule 70 provides that if a provider gives sensitive information to the Prosecutor's Office the Prosecutor can promise absolute immunity to that entity from disclosure, and, if it is disclosed, from cross-examination or further compelled disclosure pertaining to the subject matter provided to the Prosecutor under Rule 70. So they can get national security information through promises of confidentiality under Rule 70; the Defence cannot. Rule 70, on its face, does not grant the Defence any rights or opportunities to obtain or protect such information. So I would submit that whatever national security framework is developed by this appellate chamber, it should reflect on the fact that the Defence needs equal access to these materials. We need the ability to get these materials where they can be shown generally to exist and to contain exculpatory material. We need the ability to compel their production, and it is in a sense -- it is in a different, a more urgent sense that the Prosecutor needs these powers. If I could consult with my co-counsel for one moment, your Honour? (Pause). I would close with this, Mr. President, that we have had such difficulty obtaining records from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I am certain we will be seeking additional orders to try and develop and obtain these types of documents from other sources, governments, non-governmental organisations, so, of course, it goes without saying that the framework laid down is going to be tested and applied in many, many situations to come. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Before we adjourn for coffee, may I just draw your attention to Rule 70(F). You may be aware of sub-paragraph (F) of Rule 70, where it is stated that the Rules shall apply mutatis mutandis to specific information in the possession of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may look over the shoulder of my colleague? Your Honour, I am not sure when this was enacted, and secondly, the problem with that is there is frequently a chicken and egg problem. We go to an individual or government and we say we would like to see something and they say "what protections can you afford?" They are not even willing to confirm that it exists, and it is very difficult for us at that point to come back to the Trial Chamber, get some protection, take it back to the provider, and have the same kind of protections that the Prosecutor has when the Prosecutor can show the rest of Rule 70 to, for example, the Government of the United States of America, and doors open, safes open and the documents are on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we now adjourn until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I shall first of all ask whether there are any questions for Defence counsel for General Blaskic. Any questions? No. All right, so I propose that now we have the second round and so it will be, say, 15, 20 minutes for the Republic of Croatia, then the Prosecution and then we will ask the Defence counsel for General Blaskic whether they would like to add any comment. Before I call upon the Republic of Croatia to make their final closing statement, I would like to ask Judge Stephen to ask a question that Croatia may wish to address in their closing statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was one question that I had not perhaps properly understood the response to. This arises really looking at the transcript which we already have at page 72, and it arises out of the submission of Mr. Casey. Am I to understand that Croatia unequivocally asserts that if Croatia states that documents relate to national security issues that, in effect, is the end of the matter and the Tribunal's only available action then is to report the matter to the Security Council? In other words, do you deny the power of the Tribunal by any means, ex parte hearings, in camera hearings and the like, to determine for itself whether a claim made by Croatia is valid? That I understood was your submission. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mind if I -- because I forgot to make a short announcement. I was asked by the interpreters to try to speak slowly, because I understand we all speak too fast, including myself. Anyway, I thought I was speaking rather slowly, but I think it is better if we try to -- make an effort to speak as slowly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: In answer to Judge Stephen's question, what we believe the Tribunal could not do is to enter a judgment saying that Croatia was in violation of its international obligations. If the Tribunal were to face a claim of national security, there would be no reason why the Tribunal could not attempt to flesh out that claim; indeed, hold hearings. It could not require Croatia to produce the documents for its review, but it could certainly further explore the matter, so that it could then come to a conclusion itself as to whether it would then be appropriate to ask the Security Council to intervene, to essentially report what it believes is a violation to the Security Council, so it would not merely be once national security is stated nothing more can happen, but that is the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Actually, I was hoping to address this point in due turn, but if I may just briefly elaborate upon what my colleague said? Again I would try to distinguish between the specific factual point we are facing and the broad principle of law. It is my understanding that Croatia indeed has been most co-operative in dealing with this matter and will intend to do so, and it is quite conceivable that Croatia will be prepared to, if you so ruled, to convince you of the validity and sincerity of their position in this matter. That is my belief, but if you were asking me purely as a matter of international law, "Who is the final judge of the merits on one's national security?", I would only say two entities, and I think those points have actually been elucidated rather ably in the course of earlier questions; the sovereign itself and the national security council, but that is a different issue from what Croatia will do in a specific circumstance. One can envision, again hypothetically speaking, a situation where -- let us not even say Croatia, let us say any State -- might, in order to avoid the referral to the Security Council and convince you that their claims have merit, would agree to some arrangement whereby they would have Judges, and Judges only, agree to look at the merits of that case with an express proviso, and if we lose, the matter goes to the Security Council and the law should not be construed as a waiver of their -- sort of a classic appearance to contest jurisdiction. Again, in practice there can be multiple accommodations, but if a matter is posed as a pure matter of international law, then I think the answer is as we just elucidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you, that is helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Shall we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. At the outset, I promise to be very brief and speak slowly, and I want once again to take the opportunity to thank the Tribunal for the excellent hearings, superb questions and your attention to this very important issue. Let me at the outset state very briefly or restate what our position is, because again I think we all understand where we are, but I did not want us to have any confusion about it. Croatia believes and has always believed that Article 29 affixes, if you will, Croatia's international legal obligation. Croatia has always believed, and certainly believes now, that appropriate orders entered under Article 29 are legally binding on Croatia. However, Croatia also believes that the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction over States, including Croatia, primary or ancillary, expressed or implied, and consequently the Tribunal cannot issue coercive orders vis-a-vis Croatia or any other State. Again, I wanted to nail this point down because I heard slightly different references from the Prosecutor's bench as to what types of sanctions may be permissible. It is our view, as a matter of international law, that these sanctions, whether they be styled as civil, criminal, administrative or any other sanctions, cannot be entertained against States. The only remedy, and it is indeed a very serious remedy, which you have used successfully on a number of occasions, Judge Cassese, is the report to the Security Council. A brief point about ancillary jurisdiction: it is our view, and indeed I think the accepted view, that ancillary jurisdiction allows the court to reach parties that although otherwise generically within the court's jurisdictional ambit, may not be before the court at this time, and are sort of interpleaded to appear. From that perspective it is indeed the universe -- using your ancillary jurisdiction is to reach the universe of people over whom you do have a generic jurisdiction which are natural persons, and I direct your attention to Articles 6 and 8, situated in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. From that perspective, I think the Prosecutor's hypothetical -- if indeed that hypothetical was correct, he would be in a very difficult state indeed, that the only people you can reach, the accused or indicted, would not be relevant, because indeed you have full jurisdiction over any individual situated in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and in the exercise of ancillary jurisdiction you can ask them to appear. I would not repeat now the arguments made in our briefs and the points made by my colleague, but just again, one short reminder is that the concept of ancillary jurisdiction, whatever it may be, cannot be used to completely augment one's primary jurisdiction, otherwise you have a tautology and a very strange outcome indeed. As far as Articles 18, 19 and 20, to which the Prosecutor referred, I think these Articles actually, properly construed, help us. These are the Articles implementing, in our view, Articles 6 and 8, which give the Tribunal jurisdictions over individuals. They do not give the court the power over States. Point 3, and again I think we are almost there on this matter, we heard a number of excellent questions about subpoenas and why it was chosen to be a subpoena not an order, but I have heard the Prosecutor confirm a number of times that indeed they are not seeking the coercive implications that are associated, coercive powers that are associated with the word "subpoena" and out of my respect for the Prosecution I would not try to argue whether or not the coercive interpretation of a word "subpoena" is the predominant one, if one looks in the Webster dictionary and all this other stuff, but I would just say if we all agree what we are talking about is an order, without the coercive connotations thereof, let us restyle this as an order. Again, I would certainly not presume to tell you how to rule that, but it seems to me that it is almost unopposed at this point in time. We would certainly be very much pleased, because as I mentioned during the oral argument in the trial stage, among other things, it may sound quaint, but there is such a thing as dignity of States and respect for States, and perceptions are important. I think issuing subpoenas which -- even out of my respect for the Prosecutor let us say can be construed, may not be construed but can be construed, as being coercive in nature, it is not a good practice. It certainly does not advance in any practical sense what the Tribunal is trying to do. I actually was going to speak longer about state officials, but I think after Judge Cassese's excellent questions my task has been significantly simplified. The only point I would try to make again here is this: that it is two essential attributes of sovereignty, the ability to organise our internal affairs, which includes and entails ability to regulate how you conduct your intercourse with international bodies and States, so I am a little puzzled by the notion that if a given State has prescribed one motive co-operation, which on its face is perfectly legitimate and satisfactory, as Croatia has done and a number of States, which is designate an office, appoint a person to run it; in essence put that person in charge of an interagency group to perform this very vital task -- I will parenthetically add that it may be the best approach, at least my experience in government leads me to believe it, that the best way to deal with cross-cutting issues is not to rely on the regular bureaucracy -- but in any case, if a country has done that, to me, and it is working, or at least -- if it is not working then the country is not co-operating with the Tribunal, but I find it very difficult to suddenly say, "Well, we can bypass this whole machinery and address ourselves to any government official we see fit". One very brief point about our rejoinder to the Prosecutor's observation that there is no claim for any exemption for state officials in the Statute or the same point relative to national security. I do not see this Statute authorising the Tribunal, important as it is, to purport to be a comprehensive statement of international law. It is the Statute that very much operates within the existing framework of customary and treaty international law. So I would draw the exactly opposite inference from the absence of such provisions and, indeed, if principles of statutory constructions would support the same view, insofar as you do have firmly anchored recognition of principles of state sovereignty, national security, active state doctrine -- that again was described in some detail -- there is absolutely no need to provide explicit exemptions for that in the Statute. Indeed, at least American statutory interpretation practice has been such that to try to proliferate or try to restate an existing exemption is not favoured, because the implication always is that if you are repeating something that already exists, you might mean something different. I again do not draw any implications that the Prosecutor draws from the absence. Again it applies in two respects; one, no specific recognition of an active state doctrine and no specific recognition of a national security privilege. To me, the fact that there is no specific reference to it means that the baseline of existing international law that has evolved for centuries is still there. One final point. Again, the reason Croatia has invested considerable time and effort in these proceedings really stems primarily from their desire to vindicate those traditional legal principles. Croatia is a young State, it finds a great deal of solace from the principles of sovereign equality and respect for sovereignty of States, but I also think that this is not just a matter of Croatia. I am sure you would agree with me if I told you that we are talking about an enormously important international law precedent. Just from the very enumeration of all the legal doctrines that we have discussed in the course of a day, you can see what is at stake here, we are again talking about active State, we are talking about sovereign equality, we are talking about the powers of the Security Council, so you have, it seems to me, an enormously important task ahead of you and that is why Croatia is here. We thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn now to the Prosecutor? Oh, I am so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: We have just a couple of words. Your Honours, this Tribunal has been established in an attempt to help the States concerned and the re-establishment of the rule of law, not to hurt their sovereignty. In fact, the very core of the conflict in the area was disrespect of sovereignty and violation of territorial borders. Therefore it is not only a legal right but in a sense a natural right that States, demands that their sovereignty is respected. The sharp questions and far reaching questions of President Cassese are tempting me again to address a theoretical issue, that in fact the essence of sovereignty is what Mr. Rivkin has addressed, the right to establish competences in the certain State. Certainly Croatia will insist on its sovereign rights to do so. Concerning high officials, I think it has been clearly demonstrated that they cannot be held hostages in an attempt to circumvent the inability to issue subpoenas to States and in fact, I can just remember one example when subpoena would be applicable to a high state official, when acting in his official capacity, and it is the historical figure of Louis XIV, who insisted that he himself was a State. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I may now turn to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will be very brief, I only have a few points that I wish to address. Very briefly, on the question of whether or not the Security Council could be the form in which national security interest could be explored, it would be my submission that this question would not be an appropriate one for the Security Council to embark upon. It would involve not only the determination of whether a state interest was squarely engaged, but this exercise of weighing the interests of criminal justice, which are particularly fact-sensitive with respect to the facts of a particular case, and therefore would be an exercise, particularly if it was to be the kind of protracted exercise that was alluded to by Judge Stephen, would be particularly inappropriate to be conducted in the Security Council. I simply also wish to point out on the question of primary versus ancillary jurisdiction that the ancillary jurisdiction of the Tribunal over persons could not possibly limit it, as my friend has suggested, to persons under territory of the former Yugoslavia. There is absolutely no basis in the Statute to suggest that the reach of this Tribunal for testimonial or documentary evidence is so limited, in this day and age, where the conflict was being observed by all kinds of means all over the world. The access to the evidence is not limited to those who were in the former Yugoslavia and therefore could be the subject of the primary jurisdiction, the penal, criminal jurisdiction of the Tribunal. So in my submission, there is absolutely no basis upon which to import that kind of narrow reading to the Tribunal's power to access testimonial or documentary evidence. I also want to make clear, I think we have both stated our position very clearly, there is, I hope, no suggestion that we are here today because of an affront to the dignity of the State of Croatia by the use of a single word "subpoena". This cannot possibly be what is at the heart of this dispute. I continue to state that, properly interpreted, this procedural vehicle is open to the Tribunal in this particular case, but should that be perceived not to be correct, then my submission is that the order should be varied, but in a way that will convey unambiguously that the order issued is a binding order, triggering the obligation to comply by Croatia and the Defence Minister under Article 29 of the Statute. The last submission, if I may, your Honour, that I wish to make, is to address briefly the points that were made by the Defence. This is probably the place, but I do not think it is the time, to expand on the duties of the Prosecutor under the Statute. The international Prosecutor is an unique creature. There is a lot of literature dealing with the duties of prosecutors in domestic legislation, but I believe that certainly on the basis of that and on the basis of the general framework of the Statute, it is beyond dispute that the Prosecutor has a duty of fairness, and that is a duty that is triggered both in investigations and in Prosecutions and I would certainly invite the Tribunal to so conclude. I should also point out that under the Statute, the Security Council has not imposed upon States direct obligations to co-operate with the Defence in its investigative efforts. Any entitlement that the Defence may have to state assistance in the Defence of the case are triggered by its Article 21 rights and have to be expressed through the vehicle of an order of the Tribunal. Having said that, I concede that both parties, when they seek the assurance of an order of the Tribunal, must subject themselves to the intense scrutiny of the Chamber issuing the order when it is to trigger state obligations. I think it should be beyond question that before this Tribunal puts into effect these rather awesome powers of compelling a State to produce documents or any form of evidence, it should do so with the utmost caution. I also suggest that this should be exercised particularly carefully when the Defence is seeking that order, as I said, because the Statute does not impose any direct requirements of state co-operation and therefore does not assume any pre-existing relationship between the institution of the Prosecutor and the Tribunal and any particular State. These are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Defence counsel has any comments to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just to say, Mr. President, I am not sure I fully understand the import of madam Prosecutor's last comment, that there is no obligation on a State to co-operate in any way with the Defence. When we seek orders, we seek them from the Tribunal, the Tribunal issues them, if it finds them appropriate, and at that point they are an order of the Tribunal which have the full backing and authority of the Tribunal to them. They require whatever compliance, on the part of States, any order issued on behalf of the Prosecutor may require. My point in my comments was we need this process, this access to process, so that we can secure relevant proof, more than they do, because they have secret agreements with dozens of governments implementing their co-operation schemes. They have doors opened for them; we have doors closed for us. We cannot do it without the assistance of the Tribunal, so these procedures and matters that are being discussed are of critical interest to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I make just one comment? You know that in Europe, in the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, mention is always made of the basic principle of equality of arms, and this is precisely the point to which you are drawing our attention. I can assure you that this Tribunal is very keen on this principle and it will be implemented by our Trial Chambers as well. I wonder whether there are any comments by the participants or from the bench? Then before we adjourn, let me say on behalf of the Appeal Chamber that, of course, the Chamber is sensitive to the appeal made by the counsel for General Blaskic that we should not delay the trial before the Trial Chamber I of General Blaskic. I fully agree and we will heed your appeal. I promise that we will do our best -- I hope that if we work day and night, we may produce a judgment in maybe three weeks' time? I do not know whether I am too optimistic. My second point is again on behalf of the Appeal Chamber. I would like to say that I am most grateful to all those who have participated in these hearings for their lucid and helpful submissions and comments. I am really very grateful to you because I think now the Appeals Chamber is in a much better position to get together, deliberate and deliver what I hope will be a sound judgment. Thank you so much. The hearing is adjourned.
